Article Title: Caught on cam: Strike hits close to reporter live on air in Lebanon
Article Text:
The journalist and his cameraperson were injured in the strike

IDF says 'aware of reports a journalist was harmed'

Footage shows a reported Israeli air strike hitting near a Lebanese TV journalist amid concerns over renewed fighting between Israel and Hezbollah despite a June ceasefire.The incident occurred on September 6 as Al-Manar TV correspondent Ali Chbib was preparing to go on air. He was reporting from the southern Lebanese town of Nabatieh al-Fawqa when the strike hit nearby.In the footage, shared by Al-Manar, the journalist preparing for a live broadcast when the strike hit behind him. Chbib is seen ducking for cover as fire and debris rise into the air before the live TV feed cut.According to the broadcaster, both Chbib and his cameraman Mohammad Berjawi were wounded in the strike.In a statement on its Telegram channel, the Israeli military said it had carried out strikes in southern Lebanon’s Nabatieh area, killing several Hezbollah fighters following the launch of Hezbollah drones on Sunday.The Israeli military acknowledged it was “aware” of reports that a journalist was harmed “in the vicinity of the terrorist infrastructure” during the operation.“The IDF does not target uninvolved individuals or journalists under any circumstances. The IDF makes every effort to minimise harm to uninvolved individuals while maintaining the safety of its forces,” the military stated.The IDF identified Hezbollah weapons storage facilities and a command centre inside a building previously used as a hospital as targets.It also claimed to have used precision munitions and aerial surveillance to reduce harm to civilians.As many as 11 people were killed in the Israeli attacks, including nine in separate strikes in the same area.Concerns over renewed Israeli military operations have increased in Lebanon following days of strikes despite a June ceasefire aimed at halting fighting between Israel and Hezbollah.
Article Summary: Al-Manar TV correspondent Ali Chbib was preparing to go on air. He was reporting from the southern Lebanese town of Nabatieh al-Fawqa. The Israeli military said it had carried out strikes in the area. It said it killed several Hezbollah fighters following the launch of Hezbollah drones.

Article Title: In 2023, Australia paved two suburban roads with 135,000 recycled coffee cups and the equivalent of 1.2 million glass bottles, cutting the asphalt's carbon footprint by 24%
Article Text:
How coffee cups became road material

Coffee cups are particularly useful because they contain high-quality fibre.

More than just coffee cups

A road with a wider purpose

Instead of seeing a discarded coffee cup as the end of a product's life, the approach treats it as raw material for something new.

What happens to a takeaway coffee cup after the last sip? In most cases, it ends up in landfill because the thin waterproof lining inside the cup makes conventional recycling difficult. In Australia, however, thousands of these discarded cups have found a very different second life: as part of the material used to build roads.In Penrith, New South Wales, two suburban roads were resurfaced using an asphalt mixture containing recycled coffee cups, crushed glass and other recovered materials. The project used about 135,000 discarded coffee cups and the equivalent of 1.2 million glass bottles. According to Closed Loop, the recycled-content asphalt reduced the road surface's carbon footprint by about 24%.The roads, covering nearly 750 metres in total, included about 400 metres of Jamison Road in South Penrith and 350 metres of Swallow Drive in Erskine Park. The project marked an Australian-first effort to incorporate recycled coffee cups into local road construction.The technology behind the project grew out of an earlier collaboration between State Asphalt Services, recycling organisation Closed Loop and the Simply Cups program.The idea was relatively simple: take a waste stream that is difficult to recycle, recover its useful material and find a large-scale product that could use it.The idea was first explored several years before the Penrith roads were laid. John Kypreos, director of State Asphalt Services, became interested in whether discarded coffee cups could be incorporated into asphalt. His idea eventually connected with Closed Loop and its Simply Cups collection program.An early 50-metre test section was laid in western Sydney. Rather than immediately putting the material into public roads, the experimental asphalt was subjected to demanding tests. Heavily loaded trucks repeatedly drove over the test strip, while laboratory equipment flexed the material until failure.According to Kypreos, the experimental surface performed at least as well as conventional asphalt and showed strong durability. The precise proportion of coffee-cup material used in the mixture was kept commercially confidential.The resulting PAK-PAVE™ technology was subsequently developed by State Asphalts NSW with Closed Loop Environmental Solutions and the Simply Cups program. The project also involved the University of New South Wales through a Commonwealth Cooperative Research Centres Program grant and received approval from relevant NSW authorities.Coffee cups are particularly useful because they contain high-quality fibre. Their problem is not necessarily the material itself but the plastic or waterproof lining that prevents them from being easily processed through conventional paper-recycling systems.Through Simply Cups, discarded takeaway cups can instead be collected separately and processed for use in products such as road surfaces. Closed Loop founder and head Rob Pascoe has argued that recycling is only truly successful when the material collected as waste is actually turned into a product that has a market.The Penrith road surface does not rely solely on discarded cups. Crushed recycled glass also forms part of the mixture, alongside reclaimed asphalt pavement and steel furnace slag.Recycled glass has already been used in road construction across a number of Sydney councils. In the Penrith project, these recovered materials collectively account for more than half of the road-making materials, helping reduce the need for virgin resources.This is where the project moves beyond simply finding another use for rubbish. It demonstrates what environmental organisations describe as a circular economy, in which materials are kept in use rather than being discarded after a single life cycle.The concept is more demanding than simply putting something into a recycling bin. For a waste stream to genuinely be part of a circular economy, the recovered material needs to have a practical use, the resulting product needs to meet the required standards and there needs to be a viable market for it.That distinction was highlighted by Pascoe in The Guardian's 2020 report on the project. Simply collecting waste does not complete the recycling process, he argued. The material needs to be bought and used again for the loop to be genuinely closed.The coffee-cup road project also emerged at a time when Australia was grappling with how to reduce its dependence on landfill and improve domestic recycling infrastructure.The Guardian reported that Closed Loop viewed the project as part of a broader effort to find commercial uses for waste streams. The organisation's approach was to connect companies producing waste with manufacturers capable of turning that waste into useful products.The potential benefits extend beyond environmental gains. In 2020, Gayle Sloan, then CEO of the Waste Management and Resource Recovery Association Australia, told The Guardian that recovering, reusing or recycling 10,000 tonnes of waste could create substantially more jobs than sending the same material to landfill or exporting it.For State Asphalt Services, the longer-term ambition was even more ambitious: roads made almost entirely from recycled material. At the company's western Sydney plant, recycled glass was already being used as a substitute for some sand, while old road surfaces could be processed alongside other materials and incorporated into new asphalt.The Penrith project therefore represents more than an unusual experiment with coffee cups. It shows how everyday waste can become an industrial resource when collection systems, technology and a commercial market come together.Instead of seeing a discarded coffee cup as the end of a product's life, the approach treats it as raw material for something new. And in this case, that second life is literally under the wheels of Australian motorists.
Article Summary: In Penrith, New South Wales, two suburban roads were resurfaced using an asphalt mixture containing recycled coffee cups, crushed glass and other recovered materials. The project used about 135,000 discarded coffee cups and the equivalent of 1.2 million glass bottles. According to Closed Loop, the recycled- content asphalt reduced the road surface's carbon footprint by about 24%.

Article Title: Mike Niziolek spent thirty years transforming his 150-acre property into a wetland, now the former AP biology teacher is creating 'bio supermarkets' for wildlife
Article Text:
A critical project

American wetlands at risk

Mike Niziolek, a former AP biology teacher decided that he did not want to limit his impact in the world to his classrooms and wanted to do something for the planet he loves so much. This is why he has spent the past thirty years, returning his 150-acre property Elk River, Sherburne County, Minnesota to the state it was in hundreds of years ago, before humans intervened with their lives and presence on it. He has spent decades working to recreate the condition of the land hundreds of years ago.For Niziolek, this is a critical mission. Scientists estimate Minnesota has lost 50% of its original wetlands. In the southern part of the state, it's more than 90%. “In this case, we’re trying to restore them, which is a much more difficult task than saving the ones that we already have,” Niziolek said. “But we’re going to try, because it’s definitely worth the effort.”“He has been slowly and methodically transforming pastured land to oak savanna, tilled land to prairie, and ditches to wetlands,” says his bio on the Minnesota Land Trust. In 2018, the nonprofit awarded him the Landowner of the Year award. In 2024, Niziolek completed another wetland project on his land. According to him, restoring wetlands "is a much more difficult task than saving the ones that we already have."In his effort to restore the wetlands in US, Niziolek has received financial and technical help from the US Fish and Wildlife Service's Partners for Fish and Wildlife Program."We help the landowner try to manage the site in perpetuity so that they can be successful," said John Riens, a biologist with the Fish and Wildlife Service, to MPR. Together, the Fish and Wildlife Service and the Nature Conservancy have completed 72 wetland restoration projects in the last five years.But recreating a complex wetland is not as simple as digging a hole and waiting for it to fill with water. First, restoration experts analyse the site, take soil samples and look to its past. “We look at old imagery of what it might have looked like previously, or try to get a better understanding of historically what it was,” Riens said.Using that information they design a unique plan for the site and hire local contractors to remove dirt and construct the wetland. It takes time and effort to establish native plants and keep out invasive species like buckthorn, Riens said. “Then we help the landowner try to manage the site in perpetuity so that they can be successful,” he said.Despite the tremendous amount of work that goes into restoring a wetland, Niziolek sees it as a critical mission. The wetlands that he has previously restored on his property are already “teeming with life,” he said. By his estimate, 15 to 20 types of unique plants grow in this wetland he restored in the early 1990s. If he were to dip a container in the water, it would reveal countless species of invertebrates. “There are so many critters that use these spaces, either directly or indirectly. It’s amazing.”The former biology teacher says that the rich biodiversity in his and other wetlands makes them “bio supermarkets.” These attract migrating sandhill cranes and monarch butterflies, as well as providing a sanctuary for threatened species like Blanding’s turtles that are now present on his property.Furthermore, they provide protection from excess water flows from heavy rains and snowmelt, by storing floodwaters and releasing them slowly downstream. Additionally, the longer the water is held back, the more excess nutrients and sediment from runoff can be processed and filtered, improving water quality. On top of that, keeping the water on the land helps replenish the underground aquifers and provide much-needed water to plant life.Wetlands, especially those with peat bogs, are very effective at sequestering carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, making them carbon sinks, a vital tool for combating climate change. “That’s a carbon storage system that we can utilise to mitigate the human cost of climate change,” he said.Wetlands are extremely important ecosystems not only for the flora and fauna, but also the wider ecosystem and humans, providing protection from flooding and climate change along with purification and storage of water resources. However, in US wetlands are under threat in numerous parts, with the rate of loss accelerating according to a 2024 report by the US Fish and Wildlife Service.Over the ten years the report analysed, 2009 to 2019, some 670,000 acres of wetlands were lost, roughly equivalent to the land area of Rhode Island. “Wetland loss leads to the reduced health, safety and prosperity of all Americans,” said Martha Williams, Director of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.Nowadays, wetlands only cover 6% of the nation, half of the area in the 1780s. However, there is one state that has seen a net gain in wetlands in recent years thanks to conservation efforts. Minnesota, where Niziolek has been working to restore them.“I still have lots more to do, but I’m happy that this land is protected forever for future generations,” he told the Minnesota Land Trust.
Article Summary: Mike Niziolek has spent decades working to recreate the condition of the land hundreds of years ago. Scientists estimate Minnesota has lost 50% of its original wetlands. In the southern part of the state, it's more than 90%. According to him, restoring wetlands is a much more difficult task than saving the ones that we already have.

Article Title: Carl Sandburg bought a 245-acre North Carolina estate for his wife’s goat farm; it became the first National Park Service site dedicated to an American poet
Article Text:
Why the Carl Sandburg moved to North Carolina

Paula Sandburg’s goat farm was more than a hobby

The estate already had a long history

How the estate became Connemara

Carl Sandburg found a new home for his writing

The poet’s career continued to grow at Connemara

He spent his final 22 years at Connemara

How the goat farm became a National Historic Site

A farm, a family home and a literary landmark

In 1945, Pulitzer Prize-winning writer Carl Sandburg and his wife, Lilian “Paula” Sandburg, left Michigan for a 245-acre estate near Flat Rock, North Carolina. The move was driven in large part by Paula’s expanding dairy-goat operation, which needed more pasture and suitable farm buildings. Carl also wanted a warmer climate and a quieter place to write. The property, known as Connemara, offered both. More than 30 acres were available as pasture for Paula’s champion goats, while the surrounding landscape gave Sandburg the solitude he wanted. The couple and their three daughters lived there for 22 years. After Sandburg died in 1967, Paula sold the estate to the National Park Service, and Congress had already authorised it as the first NPS unit to honour a poet.The move was not simply a literary decision. Paula’s dairy-goat herd on the shores of Lake Michigan had been growing rapidly, and she needed a property better suited to running the farm. NPS records that she visited Connemara in 1945 and was impressed by its pastureland, farm buildings and setting. Carl later visited and agreed to the purchase. The estate also offered a warmer climate and a more peaceful environment for his writing.The property therefore solved two very different problems at once. It gave Paula room for her goats while giving Carl the landscape and solitude he wanted for his work.Paula had developed a serious dairy-goat breeding operation before the family ever reached North Carolina. Her prize-winning Chikaming Goat Herd was expanding rapidly in Michigan, prompting her to look for a larger and more suitable home. Connemara gave her more than 30 acres of pasture and the farm infrastructure she needed. Her herd became an important part of life at the estate, while her breeding work earned recognition beyond the property. The goats were not simply an unusual feature of a famous writer’s home. They were one of the main reasons the Sandburg family moved to North Carolina in the first place.The Sandburgs were not the first family to shape the property. The main house was built in 1838 by Christopher Memminger, a South Carolina lawyer and later Confederate secretary of the treasury. He established the estate as a summer retreat and called it Rock Hill. The property included the main house, a kitchen and two slave quarters before the Civil War. NPS records that Memminger enslaved people on the property, making slavery an important part of its earlier history.The property later passed to Ellison Adger Smythe, a wealthy textile industrialist and Confederate veteran. Smythe purchased the estate in 1900 and renamed it Connemara in reference to his family's Irish ancestry. He expanded its agricultural character, adding pastures, gardens, walking trails and livestock facilities. The estate became a full-time residence rather than simply a seasonal retreat. Smythe remained there until his death in 1942, after which the property sat unused for about three years before the Sandburgs bought it.Connemara quickly became an important part of Sandburg’s literary life. He and Paula, along with their three daughters, remained there until his death in 1967. During those 22 years, Sandburg published more than one-third of his works. He also produced Complete Poems, which earned him his second Pulitzer Prize for poetry in 1951. The estate gave him the privacy to write, but it did not isolate him completely from the surrounding community. He hiked its trails, visited local schools and read his poetry to students.Sandburg’s years at the estate coincided with several important moments in his later career. He delivered the Lincoln Day address to a joint session of Congress in 1959 and worked as a Hollywood film consultant. In 1964, President Lyndon Johnson awarded him the Presidential Medal of Freedom. The following year, he received the NAACP lifetime achievement award for his work on racial issues and social justice. By then, his reputation extended well beyond poetry. He was also known as a historian, journalist, biographer, lecturer and folksinger.Sandburg remained at the estate until his death on July 22, 1967, aged 89. The property had by then become closely associated with both his private life and his public legacy. It was where he wrote, raised his family, walked the surrounding landscape and remained connected with the local community. His life at Connemara also gave the property a significance beyond its earlier history as a plantation and later agricultural estate. It had become the home of one of America's best-known poets.After Sandburg’s death, Paula sold Connemara to the National Park Service in 1968. She also donated the family's belongings so that her husband's life and work could be preserved. That same year, Congress authorised the Carl Sandburg Home National Historic Site. NPS describes it as the first unit of the National Park Service to honour a poet. The site eventually opened to the public in 1974. What began as a family decision to find better land for a dairy-goat operation had therefore become a nationally significant literary landmark.Today, Connemara preserves several layers of American history in one landscape. It reflects the property's origins before the Civil War, its later agricultural development, Paula Sandburg’s celebrated goat-breeding work and Carl Sandburg’s final 22 years as a writer. The unusual part of the story is that the property entered the Sandburg family’s life largely because of goats, yet it ultimately became a national memorial to the man who wrote there. The 245-acre estate that once gave Paula room to expand her herd eventually became a place where visitors could trace the life and work of the “Poet of the People”.
Article Summary: Pulitzer Prize-winning writer Carl Sandburg and his wife, Lilian ‘Paula’ Sandburg, left Michigan for a 245-acre estate near Flat Rock, North Carolina. The move was driven in large part by Paula’s expanding dairy-goat operation, which needed more pasture and suitable farm buildings. Carl also wanted a warmer climate and a quieter place to write. The property, known as Connemara, offered both. The couple and their three daughters lived there for 22 years. After Sandburg died in 1967, Paula sold the estate to the National Park Service.

Article Title: In 1970, George Harrison bought Friar Park and revived its forgotten gardens; after his death, wife Olivia continued restoring its Victorian beauty
Article Text:
PC: Country Life

Friar Park became an elaborate Victorian garden experiment

Friar Park’s gardens began to decline after the war

George Harrison arrived in 1970

The neglected yews slowly returned to shape

PC: Country Life

Olivia Harrison continued the work

More than 160 plants now fill the restored topiary garden

Friar Park remains a private estate

In 1970, George Harrison bought Friar Park and discovered a grand Victorian estate whose once-famous gardens had fallen into neglect. Weeds, ivy and brambles had taken over parts of the grounds, the lake needed repairs, and the carefully shaped yews had grown into dense, unruly masses. Harrison set about restoring the landscape, clearing vegetation and bringing damaged features back into use. Gardening soon became part of daily life at the estate, shared in different ways with his family. After Harrison’s death in 2001, Olivia Harrison continued caring for Friar Park, helping restore its topiary and preserve the strange, elaborate character of its historic gardens.Long before George Harrison arrived, Friar Park had gained a reputation for its unusual gardens. The house, built in the 1870s and later enlarged, was transformed by Sir Frank Crisp, a solicitor and keen collector who developed the grounds between 1889 and 1919. His creations included a vast rock garden, grottoes, caves, underground passages and a miniature Matterhorn. In the Dial Garden, sundials replaced the fountains of a Versailles labyrinth-inspired layout. Yews were trained into columns, spirals, birds and other fanciful forms, blending plants with sculpture and inscriptions.The estate also welcomed visitors, while postcards carried its curious gardens beyond Oxfordshire.According to Country Life (British Magazine), after Sir Frank Crisp died in 1919, Friar Park passed to banker and Chinese porcelain collector Sir Percival David. The gardens remained cared for and continued welcoming visitors until the Second World War. The postwar years brought mounting costs and taxes that made large estates increasingly difficult to maintain. In 1951, Friar Park was purchased by the Salesian Sisters of St John Bosco, who established a convent school on the property. The nuns continued trimming the yews, but maintaining the extensive grounds proved costly. Plans to divide the land for development failed, leaving the sisters to put the estate back on the market.By the time Harrison bought Friar Park, the estate was far removed from the carefully maintained garden associated with Crisp. Harrison was already an internationally known musician, but the property gave him somewhere to pursue interests away from the recording studio and concert stage.The house itself required substantial repairs. Harrison later described finding parts of it deteriorating and recalled efforts being made to demolish it. He eventually helped secure its preservation as a listed building.The grounds were in an equally poor state. The lake had been used as a dumping place, while years of neglect had allowed weeds, ivy and brambles to spread through the planting. The topiary garden was particularly difficult to navigate. The old yews had expanded into dense masses, obscuring the original arrangement.Olivia Harrison said that he used garden flame-throwers to tackle some of the undergrowth and brought in two goats to help clear weeds and brambles from the rock garden. Local builders were employed to clean the lake and repair its infrastructure, including leaking areas and pipework.Once the worst of the vegetation had been removed, the structure of the topiary garden began to emerge again. Some of the yews had become almost tree-like, but the plants could withstand severe pruning.Harrison and Olivia worked on different parts of the grounds and gradually re-established the garden. New topiary forms were introduced over the years, although many of the plants were initially kept to relatively restrained shapes such as cones and columns.Gardening became part of family life at Friar Park. Their son Dhani Harrison later recalled his father spending so much time outside planting trees that, as a young child, he largely associated him with gardening rather than music.George Harrison died in 2001, but Friar Park did not become a frozen memorial to him. Olivia Harrison took on an active role in maintaining and developing the grounds.She continued adding plants and overseeing the wider estate, while also looking for ways to bring greater definition back to the topiary. Specialist topiarist James Crebbin-Bailey was brought in to work on the yews and box plants.His work went beyond simply keeping the existing shapes trimmed. Traditional forms were retained, while newer designs appeared among them, including geometric shapes and more unusual arrangements. Groups of plants were shaped into forms that sit somewhere between conventional topiary and the playful character associated with the original garden.The sundials provide one of the clearest reminders of how much was lost. Many of Crisp’s original collection had disappeared through sale or theft, and replacements have since been assembled to restore some sense of the Dial Garden.The topiary survived in a different way. Even after years of neglect, the yews could be recovered because of their ability to regenerate after hard cutting. That made it possible to work from the remnants rather than starting the garden again from scratch.Today, the topiary contains more than 160 yew and box specimens, according to estimates cited by Country Life. Most are yew, with a smaller number of box plants. Their forms vary from familiar cones and spirals to more unusual geometric and flowing shapes.Harrison's connection with Friar Park went beyond owning an unusual country house. The estate became part of his working life as well as his home, and he recorded music there during his years at the property.Yet the gardens have developed their own history alongside the music associated with the house. They began with Crisp's Victorian experiments, survived years of reduced care under later owners, and were gradually recovered after Harrison purchased the estate.
Article Summary: George Harrison bought Friar Park in 1970. The Victorian estate had fallen into neglect. Harrison set about restoring the landscape, clearing vegetation and bringing damaged features back into use. After Harrison’s death in 2001, Olivia Harrison took on an active role in maintaining and developing the grounds.

Article Title: Denmark planted trees for carbon storage, but 21 years later natural forests proved more diverse while plantations captured carbon faster
Article Text:
Image: Canva

What did scientists discover in Denmark after 21 years

Why did these plantations capture carbon faster?

Why did these plantations capture carbon faster? (Image: Canva)

Why were naturally regenerated forests more diverse?

What does the research mean for future forest restoration?

Denmark’s long-running effort to create forests on former farmland has revealed a striking trade-off between carbon storage and biodiversity. After 21 years, scientists compared naturally regenerated forests with areas deliberately planted with trees. Plantations accumulated tree biomass and captured carbon faster, while naturally colonised forests developed greater diversity and more varied ecological structures. The University of Copenhagen conducted a rare long-term comparison of two approaches to forest restoration and found why future reforestation projects may need to balance rapid carbon capture with biodiversity recovery and ecological complexity.The study ‘ Passive versus active afforestation of agricultural land: Two decades of impacts on tree biomass and ecosystem carbon storage ’ compared agricultural land that had been abandoned and allowed to regenerate naturally with areas that had been actively planted to create plantation forests. After approximately 21 years, clear differences had emerged between the two approaches. Plantation forests had accumulated substantially more tree biomass than naturally colonised forests, demonstrating that deliberate planting can accelerate early forest development and carbon storage.Naturally regenerated areas, however, developed a different ecological character as vegetation colonised the abandoned farmland without the same intensive planting approach. The researchers also compared these younger forests with mature, actively managed forests, providing a longer-term reference point. The findings show that forest recovery cannot be judged by carbon storage alone.The plantations had the advantage of being able to accumulate more biomass early in their life due to trees being purposefully planted instead of waiting for them to come naturally as part of the process of succession. This study shows that the plantation forests have 16 times more above-ground woody biomass compared to the naturally colonised forests within a period of about twenty years. As such, the faster accumulation of biomass led to faster accumulation of carbon in the trees within the early stage of forest development. It is important to note that fast biomass accumulation does not necessarily mean that the plantation mimics all the ecological features of a mature forest.The colonisation that occurred naturally enabled vegetation to grow by the means of ecological succession without any predetermined planting. This process will take more time, but will lead to greater diversity of plants in terms of their species and structure since different plants will colonise certain areas. The Danish study showed that the naturally colonised forests were distinct from the plantation in terms of vegetation and ecology, which proves the necessity of using natural factors in the process of creation of the forest. However, this statement does not mean that plantations cannot be valuable in terms of biodiversity, but only that the structure and composition of such forests differ greatly from the forests developed without planting.The results imply that there is no one particular forest restoration approach that would optimise all of the environmental benefits at once. Plantations would be an advantageous choice if the aim is to achieve rapid carbon sequestration because plantations would help to achieve faster carbon accumulation. As for natural regeneration, it would provide greater ecological diversity as the forest develops and could contribute significantly to biodiversity. Therefore, the scientists show a more complex view of afforestation that does not include only the number of trees planted.
Article Summary: Denmark’s long-running effort to create forests on former farmland has revealed a striking trade-off between carbon storage and biodiversity. Scientists compared naturally regenerated forests with areas deliberately planted with trees. Plantations accumulated tree biomass and captured carbon faster, while naturally colonised forests developed greater diversity and more varied ecological structures.

Article Title: In 1987, Kansas brought 30 bison back to Konza Prairie; 29 years later, native plant richness had risen 103% locally and 86% across catchments
Article Text:
Restoring grazing by native large herbivores such as bison can produce sustained increases in native plant diversity

How bison changed the prairie

Bison performed better than cattle

Diversity recovered after extreme drought

In 1987, 30 bison from the Fort Riley Military Reservation were brought to Konza Prairie in Kansas. Nearly three decades later, researchers found that native plant species richness had increased by 103% at the local scale and by 86% across catchments compared with areas without grazing.The findings come from a long-term study at Konza Prairie Biological Station, a large area of native tallgrass prairie in the Flint Hills of eastern Kansas, according to Kansas State University. The research compared areas grazed year-round by bison with areas grazed by domestic cattle during the growing season and areas where there were no large grazers.The study found that the increase in native plant diversity under bison grazing continued for nearly three decades. It also survived an extreme drought that affected the region in 2011 and 2012. The researchers said the gains in plant richness recovered after the drought.The bison had been introduced as part of long-term ecological research at Konza Prairie. Their grazing is studied along with other processes such as fire and climate. Unlike cattle operations in the region, the bison remain on the prairie throughout the year and are not given supplemental feed.The herd grew through reproduction, as well as additional donations, trades and purchases.Researchers found that bison grazing reduced the cover of dominant grasses over time. Four grass species can make up about 80% of annual net primary production in ungrazed areas. In the bison-grazed areas, their cover declined initially, stabilised for several years and then declined again. During the final 11 years of the study, dominant grass cover remained around 20% to 25%.At the same time, the number of native plant species increased. From 1994 to 2010, native species richness in bison-grazed areas rose by an average of 0.58 species per year at the plot scale and 1.06 species per year at the catchment scale. By 2020, native species richness was 103% higher than in ungrazed areas at the plot scale and 86% higher at the catchment scale.The researchers linked this pattern to the way bison graze. Bison mainly eat grasses and repeatedly return to areas with fresh growth. Their grazing can reduce the dominance of some grasses, allowing other plants to grow. Bison also create grazing lawns and physical disturbances such as wallows, producing different conditions across the prairie. This variation can provide opportunities for more plant species to survive.The increase in plant diversity was not driven by invasive plants. Nonnative species remained uncommon in the bison treatment, while native plants associated with prairie habitats became more frequent. Forb cover, which includes many plants that are not grasses, also increased in areas grazed by bison.The study also compared bison with domestic cattle. Cattle grazing increased native plant species richness too, but the increase was less than half that recorded under bison grazing. Compared with ungrazed areas, cattle increased native species richness by 41% at the plot scale and 30% at the catchment scale.The researchers noted that bison generally graze throughout the year, while cattle in the experiment grazed during the growing season. Bison and cattle also differ in how they choose grazing patches and what they eat. The study found that bison tend to focus more heavily on grasses, while cattle consume a greater share of nongrass plants.Earlier work at Konza Prairie had also found differences between the two animals. Bison maintain large grazing lawns and return repeatedly to them to eat new grass growth. Cattle tend to graze smaller patches more evenly across a pasture. At Konza Prairie, plant diversity was greater in bison pastures than in cattle pastures, with more forbs, particularly annual plants.One of the most important parts of the long-term study was what happened during the 2011 and 2012 drought. The two years brought one of the most extreme dry periods recorded in the Great Plains since the 1930s Dust Bowl. The researchers found that native plant richness in bison-grazed areas initially declined during the drought.However, the decline did not permanently change the long-term trend. Native species richness returned to the trajectory seen before the drought. Recovery took about four years at the plot scale and two years at the catchment scale. The researchers described this as evidence that the biodiversity gains produced by bison grazing were resilient to the extreme dry period.The researchers said greater plant diversity may help communities withstand drought because different plants use resources in different ways. Grasses at the site mainly use shallow soil water, while many forbs use deeper soil water. This difference can reduce competition when shallow soil water becomes scarce during dry conditions.The study concluded that restoring grazing by native large herbivores such as bison can produce sustained increases in native plant diversity in tallgrass prairie.
Article Summary: 30 bison from the Fort Riley Military Reservation were brought to Konza Prairie in Kansas in 1987. Nearly three decades later, researchers found native plant species richness had increased by 103% at the local scale and by 86% across catchments compared with areas without grazing.

Article Title: Soon, Aussies could opt out of social media algorithms
Article Text:
Australians could be given the option of opting out of powerful social media algorithms.

Australians could be given the option of opting out of powerful social media algorithms under new legislation cracking down on big tech, a minister said Monday. The draft law requiring a “digital duty of care” is expected to be introduced to Australia’s parliament this week.It would require firms like Meta to give users the option of turning off algorithms that tailor recommendations to their personal taste.“A lot of Australians appreciate the algorithm, both for the enjoyment they get out of it or the utility they get out of it,” communications minister Anika Wells told national broadcaster ABC. “A lot of Australians will want to choose the algorithm -- but we think that big tech should offer them the choice in the first place, and they should respect that choice.”“We should give Australians more choice over what they should see on their feeds,” she said.Social media firms have long faced scrutiny over their use of allegedly addictive algorithms and stand accused of directing users to sensational or extreme content to keep them scrolling. Australia implemented legislation barring children from social media platforms in Dec, part of a world-first crackdown designed to protect children from online bullying and “predatory algorithms”.The UK, France and others have followed suit. Data last month found that under-16s in Australia were increasing their use of social m­e­dia apps such as Instagram and TikTok despite the ban.
Article Summary: A draft law requiring a ‘digital duty of care’ is expected to be introduced to Australia’s parliament this week. It would require firms like Meta to give users the option of turning off algorithms that tailor recommendations to their personal taste.

Article Title: In 1982, Chile imported European bumblebees to pollinate crops; the invaders crossed into Argentina, spread through Patagonia, and pushed its only native bumblebee toward regional extinction
Article Text:
European bumblebees pollinating the crops. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

A second invader spread faster than expected

An alien parasite arrived with the invasive bees

Rapid Ecological Replacement of a Native Bumblebee by Invasive Species

The native bumblebee has vanished from parts of its range

Alien parasite hitchhikes to Patagonia on

invasive bumblebee

’

B. terrestris

Apicystis bombi

Greenhouse tomatoes in Chile were pollinated using imported Bombus terrestris. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Researchers are testing acoustic monitoring to track survivors

What began as a farming fix in central Chile has, over four decades, reshaped pollinator communities across southern South America. Approximately 300 queens of Bombus ruderatus were introduced into central Chile in 1982-1983 from the New Zealand population to increase the yield of red clover seeds. This farming choice led to ecological alterations that are now putting the Bombus dahlbomii at risk of regional extinction. Bombus dahlbomii is the sole bumblebee species native to the area and is one of the biggest bumblebees in the Americas.Red clover depends heavily on long-tongued pollinators, and honey bees have proved inefficient at the task. The species Bombus ruderatus was used because it had already proved successful in New Zealand's red clover fields. The scheme worked: freed from the natural enemies that had limited their numbers in Europe, the bees spread on their own and reached Patagonia, Argentina, by the early 1990s. It would take another fifteen years for Chile's greenhouse tomato industry to introduce a second European species, Bombus terrestris, which itself would take nearly another decade to disperse across the Andes and reach Patagonia.Carolina Morales, Marina Arbetman, Sydney Cameron and Marcelo Aizen documented the first records of Bombus terrestris in Patagonia, Argentina, in March 2006, after it dispersed over the Andes from Chilean greenhouses, in their 2013 article in Frontiers in Ecology and the Environment, "." Their wide survey of Patagonia found that within less than five years of its introduction, B.terrestris had become the most widespread and abundant bumblebee species in the region.Some interesting statistics can be highlighted from this evidence. During the duration of the research, B. ruderatus extended its geographical distribution up to 434 kilometers, while B. terrestris extended up to 1,320 kilometers. This southern extension of its distribution was accompanied by a retreat of B. dahlbomii. In another 20-year study of pollinators visiting the native flower Alstroemeria aurea in northern Patagonia, Aizen and colleagues found that the two exotic species had replaced the native pollinator B. dahlbomii, which had pollinated the flower for generations.Range expansion alone does not fully explain how quickly the native bee vanished from so many locations. A second line of research points to disease as a compounding factor. The study ‘(Arbetman et al., 2013), published in Biological Invasions , tested bumblebees collected before and after the arrival offor the pathogenic protozoanIn the absence of the invasion, not a single specimen of B. ruderatus or B. dahlbomii was infected by the parasite. Following the establishment of B. terrestris in the area, the situation drastically altered. Nearly one in two B. terrestris specimens tested positive for the parasite, as did just over one in two B. ruderatus specimens and about one in nine B. dahlbomii specimens. The genetic analysis revealed that the parasite belonged to the European lineage, which means that the parasite had most probably been brought in alongside the commercial bees. As noted in the study discussed above, this was the first recorded instance of Apicystis bombi infecting B. ruderatus or B. dahlbomii in the whole world.This combination of factors that are competition, the accelerated colony turnover rate of the invader and spillover pathogens has been very costly. Species B. dahlbomii has gone extinct in certain areas it used to inhabit, such as some portions of the Challhuaco Valley that scientists had been monitoring for decades. According to the information provided by the IUCN species account, this bee has not been classified in terms of its inclusion in the IUCN Red List yet. This example demonstrates the necessity of implementing regulations concerning non-indigenous pollinators. The article by Morales et al. states quite directly what this particular case study implies for future actions in other places: given how rapidly an invasive bumble bee displaces its native congener, introducing non-indigenous pollinators in areas inhabited by endangered bee species should be done much more carefully than was done in Chile in 1982.
Article Summary: Greenhouse tomatoes in Chile were pollinated using imported Bombus terrestris. Bombus dahlbomii is the sole bumblebee species native to the area and is one of the biggest bumblebees in the Americas. Researchers are testing acoustic monitoring to track survivors.

Article Title: In 1996, an Arizona hunter photographed a wild jaguar and chose not to shoot; the encounter helped inspire a project protecting a Mexican refuge
Article Text:
A jaguar (Panthera onca), in a wildlife rescue & rehabilitation centre in Formosa Province, Argentina. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

A rancher photographed a wild jaguar in 1996

Camera traps produced a first population estimate

Estimation of the density of the Near Threatened jaguar Panthera onca in Sonora, Mexico, using camera trapping and an open population model

Peloncillo Mountains on the Arizona, New Mexico. Image credits: Wikipedia

Thirteen years of data showed 48 individuals

The reserve kept growing with local support

Warner Glenn, a rancher and hunting guide, was hunting mountain lions on March 7, 1996, in the Peloncillo Mountains on the Arizona, New Mexico border when his pack of hounds cornered a large cat that he later discovered was a jaguar. He photographed the animal, and his images are recognized as the first ever taken of a wild jaguar in the United States. This adult male jaguar was not intimidated and simply sat on the bluff, watching the hounds below. Glenn was an experienced hunter and before the jaguar was listed as endangered in the United States in 1997, there was no federal prohibition on taking the animal. But instead, he decided to pull back his hounds and snap some photos of this magnificent animal.The photographs prompted biologists, including the Mexican zoologist Carlos López-González, to ask why a jaguar had appeared so far north when the species had not been seen alive in the wild in the United States for decades. The search for an origin population then took him into Sonora, Mexico, where he discovered a small, reproducing population of jaguars in the foothills of the Sierra Madre Occidental mountain range.The above-mentioned information was known to Peter Warshall, an ecologist and his wife, Diana Hadley, a historian and former rancher, who, together with other conservationists, founded the Northern Jaguar Project in 2003, as stated on the project’s website itself. With the help of the Mexican nonprofit organization Naturalia, the land of 4,000 hectares near the village of Sahuaripa was purchased to form the Northern Jaguar Reserve by taking away the cattle, according to the Northern Jaguar Project website.With jaguars impossible to count directly due to the nature of the terrain, the value of the reserve has been assessed primarily through the use of camera traps. For instance, in, published in Oryx in 2012, Gutiérrez-González, Gómez-Ramírez and López-González made use of sixteen months of camera trap photographs (February 2009 to May 2010) from the reserve and ten cattle ranches adjacent to it and identified 10 jaguars to arrive at an average density of 1.05 jaguars per 100 square kilometres based on their unique spot pattern.Another study further analyzed the data over a period of 13 years. Are Private Reserves Effective for Jaguar Conservation ? Published in PLOS ONE in 2015, the same lead researchers, along with Doherty, used the Barker robust design method, which combined closed sampling periods with resightings to estimate both apparent survival and abundance. They identified 467 jaguar photographs with 48 individuals and noted that digital cameras significantly increased the probability of detection in comparison to film cameras, with a mean density of 1.87 ± 0.47 jaguars per 100 km².The paper states that the establishment of the reserve in 2003 and its subsequent enlargements were observed, but that none of these factors can be shown to explain the change in survival estimates. Apparent survival, as reported in the 2015 PLOS ONE study, rose from 0.47 (±0.15) to 0.56 (±0.11) by 2012, a period that overlaps with the no-hunting ranch agreements adopted in 2007. The researchers stopped short of linking the rise to the reserve's presence, since jaguars are long-lived with low reproduction rates, making short-term changes hard to attribute to any single cause; they also noted that 13 years of data were still not enough to reliably detect changes in density or survival. What can be said is that neither the ranch agreements nor the sanctuary appear to have decreased survival rates.The purchased land at the core of the reserve, reported at roughly 20,000 hectares in the 2015 study, has grown since then to more than 56,000 acres (about 22,700 hectares), according to the Northern Jaguar Project's own recent reporting. That figure covers purchased reserve land only; the separate 13,000 hectares of no-hunting ranch agreements are tracked apart from it and aren't included in the acreage total. According to the Northern Jaguar Project's website, the project also operates Viviendo con Felinos, a program that pays ranchers in the region for documented camera-trap images of wild cats. The reserve still hosts a small breeding population of jaguars today.
Article Summary: Warner Glenn, a rancher and hunting guide, was hunting mountain lions on March 7, 1996, in the Peloncillo Mountains on the Arizona, New Mexico border when his pack of hounds cornered a large cat. He photographed the animal, and his images are recognized as the first ever taken of a wild jaguar in the United States. The search for an origin population then took him into Sonora, Mexico, where he discovered a small, reproducing population of jaguars in the Sierra Madre Occidental mountain range.

Article Title: In 2026, a Florida wildlife centre brought in critically endangered red-ruffed lemurs; the project is now helping restore their disappearing Madagascar rainforest
Article Text:
From a Florida wildlife centre to a rainforest in Madagascar

Why the red-ruffed lemur needs the help

The Florida lemurs are also conservation ambassadors

A wildlife centre in North Florida has welcomed two red-ruffed lemurs, turning encounters with the critically endangered animals into a way to support rainforest restoration thousands of miles away in Madagascar. The North Florida Wildlife Center in Lloyd, Jefferson County, is now home to four ruffed lemurs. Two of them, newly arrived red-ruffed lemur males, are being gradually introduced to their new surroundings and trained for the centre’s lemur encounter programme, according to WTXL and WCTV. But their role extends beyond educating visitors.The centre says proceeds and support generated through its animal encounters and conservation work help fund habitat restoration in Madagascar, including efforts to plant thousands of trees each year. Its stated goal is to plant more than 1,000 trees annually through its partnership with conservation organisation Green Again Madagascar.The connection may seem unlikely: visitors in rural Florida meet lemurs, while conservationists on the other side of the world work to restore forests.But that link is central to the wildlife centre’s conservation model. Its programmes include a partnership with Green Again Madagascar, which works with Malagasy communities on rainforest restoration, biodiversity protection and livelihoods.The centre says visits, sponsorships and donations help support both the animals in its care and conservation projects in their native habitats.For the newly arrived lemurs, that means their presence in Florida can help draw attention, and funding, to the forests on which their wild counterparts depend.The red-ruffed lemur (Varecia rubra) is found naturally only in northeastern Madagascar, particularly the forests of the Masoala Peninsula. It is classified as Critically Endangered, with habitat loss and hunting among its major threats. The species is especially dependent on intact rainforest. Red-ruffed lemurs spend much of their lives high in the forest canopy and rely heavily on fruit. They also play an ecological role as pollinators, carrying pollen between plants as they feed. That makes the loss of mature rainforest particularly damaging. When forests are cleared or fragmented, the animals lose not only shelter but also the trees and food sources that sustain them.At North Florida Wildlife Center, the animals are intended to make that distant conservation crisis more tangible. The educational encounters give visitors an opportunity to learn about red-ruffed and other ruffed lemurs while understanding why protecting their natural habitat matters. The centre also sees the animals as an educational resource for local students, particularly in a rural part of Florida where such wildlife encounters can provide an experience outside the classroom.The new arrivals are still undergoing training and conditioning before they become fully involved in the encounter programme. Their journey, however, represents more than a new attraction. Each encounter offers a chance to connect people in Florida with a forest they may never see, and, ultimately, to help put some of that forest back.
Article Summary: The North Florida Wildlife Center in Lloyd, Jefferson County, is now home to four ruffed lemurs. Two of them, newly arrived red-ruffed lemur males, are being introduced to their new surroundings and trained for the centre’s lemur encounter programme. The centre says proceeds and support generated through its animal encounters and conservation work help fund habitat restoration in Madagascar.

Article Title: Nearly 4,000 New York City students planted more than 100,000 beachgrass stalks across 2.25 acres at Coney Island Creek Park to rebuild protective dunes and help protect 50,000+ people from flooding
Article Text:
Nearly 4,000 public school students, more than 200 teachers and hundreds of community members have worked with NWF

How beachgrass can protect the coast

Coney Island Creek Park

Lessons from Superstorm Sandy

Community support and long-term work

Nearly 4,000 New York City public school students have taken part in an effort to restore protective dunes at Coney Island Creek Park in Brooklyn. Since 2022, students, teachers and community members have planted more than 100,000 American beachgrass culms across more than 2.25 acres of frontal dunes.The project is part of the Resilient Schools and Communities (RiSC) programme run by the National Wildlife Federation (NWF). According to the organisation, it combines environmental education with habitat restoration and aims to help the local community prepare for flooding and other risks linked to extreme weather.Coney Island’s coastline has faced serious flooding during major storms. Superstorm Sandy in 2012 and Hurricane Ida in 2021 highlighted the risks faced by the area. The RiSC programme was launched in 2017 in seven South Brooklyn public schools, including schools in Coney Island, to help students understand these risks and learn about the environment around them.The programme was also created to address gaps in climate education. At the time, students were receiving limited climate education, mainly through science classes, while resilience was not part of their curriculum.NWF developed a curriculum and a RiSC Vulnerability Assessment to help students understand how their schools and communities could be affected by climate-related risks and how those risks could be addressed.The restoration work focuses on American beachgrass, a native plant with a dense network of roots and rhizomes. These underground structures help the grass hold soil together. Its ability to stabilise dunes and reduce erosion has been documented, while the dunes can also provide coastal flood protection during extreme wave conditions.The beachgrass also provides cover for wildlife found in Coney Island Creek Park, including snakes, small mammals and native and migratory birds.Since 2022, habitat restoration events at the park have involved students, teachers, volunteers and community members. Nearly 4,000 public school students, more than 200 teachers and hundreds of community members have worked with NWF, NYC Parks, the American Littoral Society, corporate volunteers and Coney Islanders.The planting effort has so far restored more than 2.25 acres of frontal dunes. Teachers are also brought to the site for professional development, connecting the restoration work with environmental education.The programme aims to expand the plantings further, with the goal of building functional flood protection for more than 50,000 people living next to Coney Island Creek Park.The organisation also wants the plantings to help stop sand from moving into roads, homes and sewer drains, as clogged drains can worsen flooding on streets.The RiSC programme was shaped by what happened during Superstorm Sandy in October 2012. About 50,000 homes in Coney Island were left uninhabitable after the storm. Thousands of public housing residents were without heat and hot water for weeks, while an 11-foot storm surge brought polluted water and sand into homes and businesses.The RiSC 3.0 curriculum was developed specifically for Coney Island. It was created with community leaders, teachers and scientific advisers and looked at the area’s ecological and social history, as well as its vulnerability to coastal flooding.The programme also draws on the role of dunes in protecting coastal communities. FEMA states that primary frontal dunes are often the first line of defence against flooding in coastal regions.The plan is to continue planting native woody shrubs and trees in the maritime forest near the road. These plantings are expected to provide additional flood protection and sand stabilisation, while also creating more habitat for birds.Coney Island Creek Park has also recorded a wide range of bird species. According to NWF, eBirders have documented 244 species in the park, including grebes, loons, gulls, terns, warblers, ducks and sandpipers.Community involvement has been central to the project. In November 2025, the organisation carried out extensive outreach in Coney Island before holding a meeting where residents could learn about the RiSC programme, ask questions and provide feedback.The meeting was attended by students, community board members, representatives from four elected officials’ offices and a homeowner association. NWF said feedback towards the programme was overwhelmingly positive, while continued shoreline restoration was identified as a top priority by the local community board.The organisation has built relationships within the Coney Island community since 2020. NYC public schools have continued to support the habitat restoration work, while NYC Parks has helped with permits, staff, tools, plant material and other supplies.Emily Fano, who leads the NYC project for NWF, said the organisation learned that working in a community with a history of disinvestment required patience and trust.“I think about these four key things as a nonprofit coming into a frontline community like Coney Island that has experienced historic disinvestment: listen, be humble, earn trust, and ask what people need,” Fano said.She said residents were involved in programme planning and design as paid advisers, while local educators and volunteers received stipends.The organisation has committed to continuing its work in Coney Island until it is sure that the plantings provide functional flood protection.
Article Summary: Students, teachers and community members have planted more than 100,000 American beachgrass culms across more than 2.25 acres of frontal dunes. The project is part of the Resilient Schools and Communities (RiSC) programme run by the National Wildlife Federation. It combines environmental education with habitat restoration to help the local community prepare for flooding.

Article Title: Amazon cargo jet pilots tried to abort unstable landing before plane overran Miami runway
Article Text:
An Amazon cargo plane lies damaged near a parking lot two days after overshooting a runway at Miami International Airport, Tuesday, Sept. 8, 2026, in Miami. (AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell)

Did pilots hesitate?

(With AP inputs)

Pilots of an Amazon cargo jet that overshot the runway at Miami International Airport had tried to abort an unstable landing, according to information released by investigators on Tuesday (local time).Upon landing, the plane overshot the runway and crashed into a van, killing five people inside. The accident occurred on September 13, and the flight recorders were recovered a day later.The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) is investigating the crash. Investigators will interview the pilot, co-pilot and crew members on Wednesday as they seek to determine why the jet overran the runway.The crash injured five other people, two of whom remain in critical condition while a third is in stable condition. The pilot and co-pilot have since been released from hospital.Miami-Dade Sheriff identified the deceased as Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo, 53; Julio C. Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47.The Amazon jet was landing after a two-hour flight from Puerto Rico as storms brewed around Miami airport. According to the NTSB, the plane barrelled roughly 1,300 feet (396 metres) past the end of the runway.According to Mike O'Donnell, a former Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the fact that the plane landed on its nose and right landing gear first indicated an unstable landing. He suggested the pilot might have been attempting a “go-around” to retry the landing approach.“A go-around probably should have been executed sooner than that. And it seems like they hesitated,” he added.By the time the crew tried to abort the landing, O’Donnell noted, it may have been too late if there wasn’t enough runway left. However, interviews investigators have scheduled with the pilots for Wednesday are expected to provide more insight into what they were thinking at that moment.Aviation attorney Mary Schiavo, a former Transportation Department inspector general, observed that “it almost seems like there was a disagreement between the pilots on what to do.”Video of the landing showed the plane hovering above the runway for a long time without flaring the nose to bring the wheels onto the ground. Experts said it appeared a strong tailwind propelled the plane far past the point where it was supposed to land. Air traffic controllers had also not changed the approach to the runway to allow the plane to land into a headwind.Meanwhile, two of the Miami airport’s four runways remained closed on Tuesday and will not reopen until NTSB investigators have gathered all the information they need from the crash site.More than 225 flights have been cancelled since Sunday, while hundreds more have been delayed.
Article Summary: Pilots of an Amazon cargo jet that overshot the runway at Miami International Airport had tried to abort an unstable landing, according to information released by investigators. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) is investigating the crash. Investigators will interview the pilot, co-pilot and crew members on Wednesday as they seek to determine why the jet overran the runway.

Article Title: Gene Autry bought a 110-acre California movie ranch in 1952; a massive fire destroyed 54 buildings before he finally sold the last 10 acres
Article Text:
PC: Official website

Melody Ranch began as a Hollywood Western film studio in 1915

Gene Autry turned Melody Ranch into a television Western hub

PC: CLUI

The Melody Ranch fire wiped out much of Autry’s Western collection

After the fire, Melody Ranch slowly passed out of Autry’s hands

Old photographs helped restore Melody Ranch’s Western street

A museum keeps Melody Ranch’s Hollywood history on display

Melody Ranch after the studio years

Before Melody Ranch became associated with Gene Autry, it was already part of the machinery of early Hollywood. The Newhall property opened in 1915 as Monogram Studios, providing a ready-made setting for Western films at a time when the genre was becoming a staple of American cinema. John Wayne was among the performers whose early productions used the site. Autry had filmed there himself before purchasing it in 1952. Under his ownership, the ranch was renamed Melody Ranch and adapted to the demands of television, with several Flying A Pictures series made on its sets.The property later hosted a long list of Western programmes, from Hopalong Cassidy to Gunsmoke. Then a fire swept through Placerita Canyon in 1962. Fifty-four structures were destroyed, along with much of Autry's collection. What followed was not a clean ending, but decades of selling, rebuilding and changing use.The property was already established as a movie location when Gene Autry acquired it. Known as Monogram Studios, the Newhall ranch had opened in 1915, during the formative years of the Western film industry. Its sets were used for early Western productions, including a number of John Wayne's Lone Star Monogram films.Autry himself had a connection to the site before he owned it. His 1935 film Tumbling Tumbleweeds, made for Republic Pictures, was among the productions associated with the ranch.By the time Autry bought the property in 1952, the place had accumulated a useful collection of Western settings. That made it suitable for the new television market, where producers needed locations that could be redressed and reused without building an entire town for every production.Autry renamed the property Melody Ranch and turned much of its attention towards television.The ranch became the base for several of Autry's Flying A Pictures productions. The Gene Autry Show was filmed there, as were The Range Rider, Annie Oakley, Buffalo Bill, Jr. and The Adventures of Champion.Other Western series passed through the gates. Hopalong Cassidy, Wild Bill Hickok, Wyatt Earp, The Cisco Kid, Sheriff of Cochise and Gunsmoke all used Melody Ranch at various points. The property was not limited to television either. Feature films continued to use its sets, including Fred MacMurray's At Gunpoint in 1955, as reported.The ranch offered a ready-made Western environment, with streets, buildings and open areas that could serve different productions. Camera crews could find useful angles without having to construct an entirely new setting.Autry also appeared there with Champion, the horse who became one of the most recognisable animals associated with his career. Photographs from the 1950s show the pair on the ranch's Western street.For Autry, Melody Ranch was more than a place where productions could be made. He had accumulated a substantial collection connected with his career, including antique automobiles, stagecoaches, costumes, documents, recordings and other memorabilia. He was considering turning the property into a Western museum.According to the official website of Gene Autry, that plan changed on August 28, 1962. A major fire swept through Placerita Canyon in Newhall and reached the ranch. Fifty-four structures on the 110-acre property were destroyed. The losses extended well beyond the buildings themselves. Autry's collection of vehicles and stagecoaches was badly affected, as were his wardrobe and costumes, papers and other material. An archive containing about 17,000 recordings was also lost.Several parts of the ranch escaped the destruction. The adobe house survived, along with another house, the adobe village, a schoolhouse, a cabin and the main entrance.The fire effectively ended Melody Ranch's period as a large working film and television property under Autry.Autry abandoned his plans for a museum and the ranch entered a much quieter period. Over the following three decades, he gradually sold most of the property to developers.The landholding became a fraction of what it had been. The original ranch covered 110 acres; eventually only a small remnant remained in Autry's hands.Champion Three, rather than film production, became an important part of the property's later story. The horse remained at Melody Ranch until his death in 1990. After that, Autry sold the remaining ranch to brothers Renaud and Andre Veluzat.The Veluzat family already had deep connections with film locations in the Santa Clarita Valley. Their family had operated a film ranch in Saugus since the early 1950s, and the brothers took on the task of bringing Melody Ranch back into use.Restoration meant working from what little remained and from the visual record of the ranch's earlier years. The Veluzats used old photographs and videotapes to reconstruct the Western street and church sets, aiming to recreate their appearance from the early television period.There was one practical alteration. The rebuilt street sits slightly higher than the original version. That change was made for the camera rather than historical accuracy, helping keep the residential development on the hill north of the ranch out of shots.The restored street eventually returned to television production. Among the programmes to use the setting was HBO's Deadwood, giving the old ranch another connection with Western screen history decades after Autry's productions had ended.The property also retains a museum devoted to its film history. Its collection includes vintage automobiles, photographs, Champion's training hoop and other material from the ranch's years in the entertainment business. Visits are arranged by appointment rather than through ordinary daily opening hours.The surviving site is therefore considerably smaller than the place Autry purchased in 1952. The 110-acre ranch that once accommodated a busy collection of film and television productions was progressively reduced through development and sale, leaving only a small portion of the original property.Yet the surviving sets preserve something of the ranch's working appearance. Buildings that were once scenery for weekly television programmes became historic pieces of a California film landscape.Melody Ranch also developed a life outside film production. Since 1994, it has hosted the Santa Clarita Cowboy Poetry and Music Festival each March. The event brings performers, musicians and visitors to the ranch, alongside Western-themed displays, food and merchandise.The ranch's history is unusually layered for a surviving film location. It began in the silent-era and early Hollywood period, became part of Autry's television operation, was heavily damaged by fire, passed out of his ownership and was eventually restored by a family already familiar with the business of maintaining film ranches.What remains is not the 110-acre property Autry bought. It is a much smaller piece of it, shaped by decades of production, fire, development and restoration. The Western street, rebuilt from photographs and old footage, provides the most visible reminder of the ranch's former role. Beneath that scenery is a longer story about how quickly a working Hollywood location can disappear, and how parts of it can still be reconstructed many years later.
Article Summary: Melody Ranch opened in 1915 as Monogram Studios in Newhall, California. John Wayne, Annie Oakley, Buffalo Bill, Jr. and The Adventures of Champion all filmed there. In 1952, Gene Autry bought the property and turned it into a TV Western hub. A fire in 1962 destroyed much of the property, including Autry's collection.

Article Title: Georgia O'Keeffe bought a small Ghost Ranch home in 1940 and spent decades painting the surrounding desert; a conservation plan is now protecting 6,000 acres from development
Article Text:
For the unversed, Ghost Ranch sits amid the dramatic red and yellow cliffs of the Piedra Lumbre, about 65 miles northwest of Santa Fe along U.S. 84. The region became closely associated with O’Keeffe, whose paintings transformed its cliffs, mesas, bones and expansive skies into some of the most recognizable images in American art.

A legacy supported by public funding

Preserving the Ghost Ranch experience

The landscape behind O’Keeffe’s Art

A vision that continues

Poll Vote & Share your view What is the main benefit of protecting the land around Ghost Ranch? Preserving its natural beauty Protecting its artistic heritage 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Long before the desert landscapes of Northern New Mexico became icons of American art, they were simply a vast meeting of red cliffs, golden mesas, open skies and rugged wilderness. For artist Georgia O’Keeffe, that landscape became both a home and a source of inspiration. Now, decades after she first made Ghost Ranch part of her life, a new conservation effort is working to ensure the scenery that shaped her art remains largely unchanged for generations to come. The National Ghost Ranch Foundation and the Presbyterian Foundation announced a partnership with the State of New Mexico and the New Mexico Land Conservancy in 2025 to protect approximately 6,000 acres surrounding Ghost Ranch. According to a report by Presbyterian Foundation, under the Ghost Ranch Conservation Plan, the land, water and wildlife habitat are being protected through conservation easements. These voluntary agreements safeguard land for conservation purposes while allowing its owners to retain ownership, the report states. The goal has been not only to protect the area's natural beauty but also to ensure Ghost Ranch can continue operating its educational and retreat programs sustainably for years to come.The first phase of the conservation effort received $930,000 from New Mexico's Natural Heritage Conservation Act Program through the Energy, Minerals & Natural Resources Department. The funding came from the Land of Enchantment Legacy Fund, a state initiative supporting land and water conservation, agriculture and outdoor recreation. According to the report, the money helped cover transaction costs associated with establishing the conservation easements. The New Mexico Land Conservancy helped held the easements in trust for public benefit and traditional land users, working with the Presbyterian Foundation, the National Ghost Ranch Foundation and the State of New Mexico.According to the same report, the conservation plan is designed to protect the surrounding landscape without changing the core visitor experience. The easements is said to not cover the 550 acres containing Ghost Ranch's main facilities, including its visitor center, trails, lodging, stables and museums. That distinction means the thousands of people who visit Ghost Ranch each year can continue to explore and experience the site while the larger surrounding landscape receives long-term protection from development. New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham has called the initiative an opportunity to preserve the vistas that attracted O’Keeffe to the region and continue to define Northern New Mexico's distinctive character.For the unversed, Ghost Ranch sits amid the dramatic red and yellow cliffs of the Piedra Lumbre, about 65 miles northwest of Santa Fe along U.S. 84. The region became closely associated with O’Keeffe, whose paintings transformed its cliffs, mesas, bones and expansive skies into some of the most recognizable images in American art.O’Keeffe bought a small house and seven acres at Ghost Ranch in 1940 and also maintained a larger home and studio in nearby Abiquiú. Those properties are now separately owned and managed by the Georgia O’Keeffe Museum in Santa Fe. While the new conservation plan does not directly protect those properties, it preserves many of the landscapes that inspired her work, including views toward Abiquiú Lake, the Rio Chama and Cerro Pedernal, known in Tewa as Tsip’in.Ghost Ranch's conservation story stretches back generations. Arthur and Phoebe Pack donated the land in 1955 to the Board of Christian Education, now part of the Presbyterian Foundation. Their vision was to preserve Ghost Ranch as an educational and retreat center while protecting its surrounding lands. The new conservation plan carries that vision forward. By bringing government agencies, nonprofit organizations and landowners together, the partnership aims to ensure that the landscape O’Keeffe found so compelling remains a place of nature, culture, learning and inspiration, rather than becoming another developed piece of the American West.Images Courtesy: Wikipedia and Presbyterian Foundation
Article Summary: Ghost Ranch sits amid the dramatic red and yellow cliffs of the Piedra Lumbre, about 65 miles northwest of Santa Fe along U.S. 84. The region became closely associated with O’Keeffe, whose paintings transformed its cliffs, mesas, bones and expansive skies into some of the most recognizable images in American art. A new conservation effort is working to ensure the scenery that shaped her art remains largely unchanged.

Article Title: A Napa art center is giving up development rights on 162 of its 217 acres; the deal protects 75% of the estate while directing up to $1.85 million back to the arts
Article Text:
What happens to the remaining land

A future trail to Milliken Peak

Preserving more than a view

A major conservation agreement in California’s Napa Valley is set to permanently protect much of the sprawling landscape surrounding the di Rosa Center for Contemporary Art, while potentially providing the institution with up to $1.85 million to support its cultural operations. Announced August 25 by the Land Trust of Napa County, the deal brings together the di Rosa Center and the Napa County Regional Park and Open Space District in an effort to preserve both the land and the arts center’s long-standing connection to it.The agreement covers 162 acres of di Rosa’s 217-acre property in the Carneros region, placing roughly three-quarters of the estate beyond future private development. The protected area includes Milliken Peak, a 732-foot summit with sweeping views across Carneros, as well as watershed areas, wildlife habitat, and the hillsides surrounding the center’s cultural campus.The move is particularly significant for di Rosa, whose identity has always been rooted in the relationship between art and nature. The center describes its property as a 217-acre destination featuring galleries, a lake, walking trails and outdoor sculptures.
