Under the new arrangement, the surrounding landscape will be preserved as public open space, reinforcing the very setting that has helped define di Rosa for decades.The deal does not mean di Rosa is giving up its entire Napa operation. The center will retain ownership and programming on roughly 53.5 acres that make up its principal cultural campus. That area includes the galleries and other facilities that support its exhibitions and public programs.The Land Trust of Napa County will hold the permanent conservation easement over the 162 acres, while the Napa County Regional Park and Open Space District is expected to own and operate the future public parkland. The financial arrangement is also designed to help di Rosa remain viable. An initial $500,000 allocation is secured for the arts center, while another $1.35 million would be available if voters approve Measure B in November. Together, that could bring the support connected to the deal to $1.85 million.One of the most intriguing parts of the plan is what could eventually happen on the protected hillsides. Plans envision a roughly two-mile trail leading to the summit of Milliken Peak. If completed, it would create a new public hiking destination while opening up views that are currently inaccessible to most visitors.The landscape would also remain closely tied to the art center’s identity. di Rosa has historically incorporated large-scale sculptures into its grounds, including works in its Sculpture Meadow leading toward Milliken Peak. Its existing programming includes guided hikes that combine the property’s art and natural surroundings. The future trail could take that concept further, with plans to place additional large sculptures from the di Rosa collection along the route.For now, however, the ridge remains temporarily closed while planning for the future park continues. di Rosa is expected to continue offering its regular hiking programs in the meantime.The significance of the agreement extends beyond keeping an attractive Napa ridgeline undeveloped. The Land Trust describes the property as part of an ecological corridor, with the conservation easement helping protect habitat and local watersheds. The arrangement also fits into a much longer history of conservation around di Rosa: the center says its property has been protected through Napa County land-trust conservation measures while continuing to function as an art destination.For Napa, the result could be an unusual combination: land that becomes increasingly accessible to the public without losing the artistic character that made the property distinctive in the first place. If Measure B receives voter approval in November, the proposed funding would also give di Rosa additional resources to maintain its cultural mission while the surrounding hillsides move toward their future as public open space. In a region where land, development, conservation and culture frequently compete for space, the di Rosa agreement attempts to make all four coexist on the same 217 acres.
Article Summary: A major conservation agreement in California's Napa Valley is set to permanently protect much of the sprawling landscape surrounding the di Rosa Center for Contemporary Art. The agreement covers 162 acres of di Rosa’s 217-acre property in the Carneros region, placing roughly three-quarters of the estate beyond future private development. Plans envision a roughly two-mile trail leading to the summit of Milliken Peak. If completed, it would create a new public hiking destination while opening up views that are currently inaccessible.

Article Title: A North Florida family permanently protected 816.46 acres with a $2.665 million easement; farming can continue while the land stays undeveloped inside a 1.6-million-acre wildlife corridor
Article Text:
Representative image

A landscape of forests, fields and water

The choice to protect while farming

In a 1.6 million acre wildlife corridor

Benefits for water and wider ecosystems

A model for private land conservation

Looking to the future

In the rolling pine forests and pasturelands of Putnam County, a North Florida family has made a decision that will change the landscape for generations to come. They have placed a permanent conservation easement on 816.46 acres of their working farm, locking in protection for a sprawling tract of forests, wetlands and agricultural fields.Valued at $2.665 million, the easement ensures that the land will never be subdivided or developed, even as farming and ranching activities continue under sustainable management. The property lies within a much larger 1.6 million-acre wildlife corridor that links some of the most important natural areas in the Southeast.As reported by Action News Jax, the deal is a striking example of how private landowners can help safeguard habitat and rural character while keeping their land in production.The 816 acres sit in the heart of North Florida’s working lands country, a region where cattle graze beneath longleaf pines, cypress domes rise from flatwoods, and blackwater creeks wind toward the St. Johns River. The property includes a mix of habitats, from upland pine forests and hardwood hammocks to seasonal wetlands and open pastures. This variety supports a wide array of wildlife, including white-tailed deer, wild turkey, bobcats, black bears and numerous bird species that rely on large, unbroken tracts of forest and field.From a conservation perspective, the value of the land is not just in its size, but also in its location. It is part of a designated wildlife corridor that runs through much of North and Central Florida, connecting national forests, state parks, wildlife management areas, and other conserved lands. These corridors allow animals to travel safely across the landscape, find mates, reach seasonal resources, and respond to changing conditions such as climate change or habitat disturbance.For the family that owns the land, the choice to put a conservation easement in place was not a choice to stop farming. It was a choice to ensure that farming could continue without the pressure of future development. Under the terms of the easement, the land remains in private ownership and can still be used for agriculture, timber production, and other rural pursuits. What changes is the right to subdivide the property into smaller lots or build residential or commercial structures beyond what is needed for normal farm operations. This approach recognises that working lands are themselves a form of conservation.Well-managed pastures and forests provide habitat, store carbon, filter water and maintain the open character that defines much of rural Florida. By protecting the land from development while allowing continued agricultural use, the easement supports both ecological and economic goals. The financial value of the easement was the difference between the value of the land as developable property and the value of the land as restricted, working land, and was appraised at $2.665 million. The landowner can receive financial benefits for donating or selling the easement (including possible tax benefits), while providing long-term conservation benefits.The bigger picture for this easement is a 1.6 million acre wildlife corridor that crosses several counties in North and Central Florida. This corridor is part of a larger network of protected and working lands that are meant to maintain connectivity for species that require large ranges, like black bears and Florida panthers. As development creeps in and fragments habitat, these corridors are more and more important to allow animals to safely travel through human-dominated landscapes. By adding their 816 acres to the permanent protection portfolio, the family has effectively strengthened an important link in this corridor.The property helps to fill gaps between other protected areas, reducing the chances that animals will become isolated in small parcels of habitat. For species that need to travel long distances to find food, mates or new territories, even a single large tract can make the difference between a functional landscape and a broken one. Conservation groups and state agencies have identified this corridor as a priority for protection because of its role in maintaining regional biodiversity and ecological resilience. Each new easement or protected area within the corridor adds to a growing mosaic of lands that collectively function as a much larger reserve.Beyond its value for wildlife, the protected land plays an important role in the region’s water systems. North Florida’s flat terrain means that water moves slowly across the landscape, soaking into the ground, recharging aquifers and filtering through forests and wetlands before reaching rivers and springs. These forests and undisturbed soils on the easement property absorb rainfall, slow down runoff and trap sediments and nutrients that would otherwise wash into nearby water bodies. This natural filtration helps keep the health of the St. Johns River and its tributaries strong, which are vital for fisheries, recreation and drinking water supplies. They also provide a buffer from flooding by slowing the movement of water during heavy rains. As climate change increases the frequency of extreme weather events, these ecosystem services are even more important.The land also contributes to carbon storage, especially the mature forests and wetland soils. When they’re protected and managed properly, those places will continue to serve as carbon sinks, helping to counterbalance some of the greenhouse gasses behind climate change.The Putnam County easement demonstrates how private landowners can take a leadership role in conservation without relinquishing ownership or traditional land uses. In a state where much of the land is privately held, the choices of individual families and ranchers have outsized importance for the fate of wildlife and natural resources. Conservation easements offer a flexible tool that can be tailored to the specific goals of the landowner while delivering public benefits.For other landowners in the wildlife corridor and beyond, the deal shows that protection and production are not mutually exclusive. It is possible to farm, ranch and manage timber while also committing to keep the land undeveloped in perpetuity.This dual focus can help sustain rural economies, preserve cultural traditions and maintain the open landscapes that many people value about Florida’s countryside. Conservation organisations and state agencies often work with landowners to identify properties that are especially important for connectivity, habitat quality or water resources. When a willing partner emerges, as in this case, the result can be a win-win for nature and for the people who live on and care for the land.With the easement recorded, the immediate work of protection is complete, but the long-term task of stewardship is just beginning. The land will require monitoring to make sure that the terms of the easement are being honored and that management practices continue to support agricultural productivity and ecological health. This may involve periodic inspections, coordination with conservation holders and adjustments to grazing, timber harvest or other activities as conditions change. For the family, the easement represents a legacy decision, a way of honouring their connection to the land while ensuring that it remains intact for future generations. For the wider region, it is a building block in a much larger effort to keep Florida’s wildlife corridors functional, and its working lands viable.In a time when development pressures are strong and natural habitats are increasingly fragmented, stories like this one offer a different path. They show that private landowners, with the right tools and support, can help shape a landscape where farming and nature coexist, and where the open spaces that define North Florida endure well beyond any single lifetime, providing lasting benefits for wildlife, communities and future generations.
Article Summary: A North Florida family has placed a permanent conservation easement on 816.46 acres of their working farm. The property lies within a 1.6 million-acre wildlife corridor that links some of the most important natural areas in the Southeast. The easement ensures that the land will never be subdivided or developed, even as farming and ranching activities continue.

Article Title: Cox Enterprises gave up development rights on nearly 4,400 South Carolina acres worth hundreds of millions; the land is now protected forever, including 40 miles of river and marsh frontage
Article Text:
Representative image

A landscape of rare scale and quality

The decision to protect the land

What the easement covers

Why this matters for wildlife

Benefits for water and people

A model for large-scale conservation

In the low country of South Carolina, where blackwater rivers wind through cypress swamps and marshes give way to the Atlantic, a quiet but monumental act of conservation has just reshaped the landscape. Cox Enterprises, a major media and communications company, has donated development rights on nearly 4,400 acres of its Clarendon Farms property, locking in permanent protection for one of the most ecologically rich tracts in the Southeast. The land, valued at hundreds of millions of dollars, includes about 40 miles of river and marsh frontage that provide critical habitat for fish, waterfowl and countless other species. As announced by Ducks Unlimited, the donation marks one of the largest and most significant conservation easements in United States history, ensuring that this vast expanse of forests, wetlands and working farmland will remain undeveloped in perpetuity.Clarendon Farms sits in the heart of South Carolina’s coastal plain, a region known for its biodiversity, productive fisheries and deep hunting and fishing traditions.The property spans a mosaic of habitats, from mature bottomland hardwood forests and pine stands to expansive freshwater marshes and tidal creeks. Blackwater rivers such as the Santee and its tributaries flow through the land, carrying tannin-stained water that supports distinctive plant and animal communities.What makes Clarendon Farms especially remarkable is its size and continuity. In a part of the country where large tracts have been subdivided for housing, timber plantations or commercial development, 4,400 acres of intact, well-managed land is increasingly rare. The 40 miles of river and marsh frontage multiply its ecological value, creating long corridors of habitat that allow wildlife to move, feed and breed across a wide area.For Cox Enterprises, the path to permanent protection began with a recognition that the land’s long-term value extended beyond potential real estate development, as per the report. The company had owned and managed Clarendon Farms for decades, using it for timber production, hunting leases and wildlife management. Over time, leaders within the organisation came to see the property as a legacy asset, one that could deliver lasting benefits for conservation, recreation and local communities if kept intact. The chosen approach was a conservation easement, a legal agreement in which the owner of the property voluntarily relinquishes certain rights of development but retains ownership of the land.In this case, Cox relinquished rights to subdivide or build on the property in the future. The easement is monitored by qualified conservation organisations that are responsible for managing the land and ensuring that the easement conditions are met by current and future owners of the property. By giving up development rights valued at hundreds of millions of dollars, Cox made a financial sacrifice in the traditional sense. Yet the company frames the decision as an investment in natural capital, one that yields returns in the form of clean water, wildlife habitat, carbon storage and public goodwill.The conservation easement on Clarendon Farms is comprehensive in scope. It restricts residential, commercial and industrial development across the nearly 4,400 acres, preserving the land’s open, forested and wetland character. Timber harvesting and other traditional land uses can continue under sustainable management plans, but they must be carried out in ways that protect water quality, wildlife habitat and the overall ecological integrity of the property. A major focus of the easement is the protection of aquatic resources. The 40 miles of river and marsh frontage include critical spawning and nursery areas for fish such as striped bass, catfish and shad, as well as foraging grounds for wading birds, waterfowl and otters. The easement also helps to maintain natural water flows, sediment transport and nutrient cycling that help sustain the health of the entire watershed by keeping these shorelines free from docks, bulkheads and dense development. The agreement also protects cultural and historical resources on the land, including sites associated with indigenous peoples and earlier periods of European American settlement. These features add another layer of significance to a property already remarkable for its natural values.For wildlife, the permanent protection of Clarendon Farms is transformative. The South Carolina low country is a key part of the Atlantic Flyway, a migratory route used by millions of birds each year. Waterfowl such as wood ducks, teal and geese rely on the region’s flooded fields, marshes and bottomland forests for food and shelter during migration and winter. By keeping large blocks of habitat intact and well managed, the easement helps ensure that these species have places to rest and refuel as they travel thousands of miles.The property is also important for game species such as white-tailed deer and wild turkey, which thrive in the mix of mature forest, early successional habitat and agricultural openings found on Clarendon Farms. For fish, the protected river and marsh frontage provides critical connectivity between upstream spawning areas and downstream estuaries supporting life cycles that span the entire river system. In an era of accelerating habitat loss and climate change, large, connected landscapes like this are increasingly seen as refuges where wildlife can persist and adapt. The easement effectively locks in that function for generations to come.The ecological benefits of protecting Clarendon Farms extend well beyond the property’s borders. Forests and wetlands serve as natural filters, trapping sediments and nutrients that would otherwise enter rivers and eventually flow into coastal estuaries. This keeps the water clear and clean, which supports fisheries, shellfish beds and recreational activities like fishing and boating. The land also helps to reduce flooding. In times of heavy rainfall, bottomland forests and marshes absorb and slowly release water, lowering peak flows downstream and reducing flood risks for nearby communities. As climate change increases the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, this buffering capacity becomes ever more valuable.For people, the protected land offers opportunities for hunting, fishing, birdwatching and nature study, though public access may be limited depending on the terms of the easement and the policies of the landowner and managing organisations. Even without broad public entry, the existence of a large, undivided tract contributes to the character of the region and supports local economies tied to outdoor recreation and natural resource-based industries.The Clarendon Farms easement is being hailed as one of the most significant private land conservation actions in recent US history. Its scale, ecological quality and permanent nature set a high bar for what is possible when landowners, conservation groups and public agencies align around a shared vision. For other major landowners, particularly corporations with large real estate holdings, the donation provides an appealing model. It demonstrates that land protection can be compatible with good business sense, reputation for the brand, and long-term value creation. It also demonstrates that conservation does not necessarily imply public acquisition or government ownership. Private lands can stay in private hands and still provide public benefits through carefully crafted easements. Conservation organizations talk of the Clarendon Farms deal as proof that breakthroughs are still possible, even in areas where development pressure is high, and land prices are steep. The trick is finding partners who appreciate the inherent and practical value of keeping large landscapes whole.” Looking ahead With the easement in place, the work turns to stewardship. It will take continued attention and resources to monitor the property to ensure the terms of the easement are being met, to manage forests and wetlands for wildlife and water quality, and to adjust to evolving conditions, such as sea level rise and species distribution changes. For Cox Enterprises, the donation closes one chapter and opens another. The company no longer holds the option to develop Clarendon Farms, but it gains a lasting role in the story of one of the Southeast’s most important conservation landscapes. For wildlife, water and the people who depend on them, the protection of nearly 4,400 acres and 40 miles of river and marsh frontage is a promise that this special place will endure, not just for the next few decades, but forever.
Article Summary: Cox Enterprises donated development rights on nearly 4,400 acres of its Clarendon Farms property. The land, valued at hundreds of millions of dollars, includes about 40 miles of river and marsh frontage that provide critical habitat for fish, waterfowl and countless other species. The donation marks one of the largest and most significant conservation easements in United States history.

Article Title: 'Break pattern of impunity': UN experts flag persecution of Pakistan's Ahmadiyya community
Article Text:
Poll Vote & Share your view How should the Pakistani government address human rights violations against minorities? Strengthen laws and policies Increase community awareness programs Collaborate with international organizations All of the above 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

United Nations experts have expressed concerns over reports of human rights violations against members of the Ahmadiyya Muslim community in Pakistan and urged authorities to ensure their protection.According to an official release, the experts said, "We are deeply concerned by persistent reports that members of the Ahmadiyya community continue to face harassment, criminal prosecution, violence, and exclusion because of their religious identity.""Every individual has the right to freedom of thought, conscience, religion or belief. No one should be subjected to discrimination, intimidation, or violence, nor should they be prevented from peacefully manifesting their faith or face discrimination with respect to any of their human rights," they added.Experts also highlighted ongoing attacks on Ahmadi places of worship; desecration of graves; interference with peaceful religious observance, including in the context of Eid-ul-Fitr and Eid-ul-Adha; arrests and prosecutions related to religious practices or identity; and hate speech."The State has a responsibility to exercise due diligence to prevent human rights violations, investigate allegations promptly and impartially, prosecute those responsible in accordance with international standards, and provide effective remedies to victims," the experts said.“Pakistan must break the pattern of impunity that has allowed perpetrators of attacks and incitement to hatred and violence to act without restraint,” they said. “These attacks take place with tacit official complicity, whilst the cycle of fear prevents people and institutions from upholding the rights and dignity of these minority groups.”They called on the Pakistan government to ensure that all individuals, regardless of their religion or belief, enjoy equal protection under the law without discrimination. The experts also urged the government to review legislation and administrative measures that may be inconsistent with its obligations under international human rights law, including the rights to freedom of religion or belief, freedom of expression, freedom of association and assembly, cultural rights, and equality before the law."Combating religious intolerance requires more than responding to individual incidents," the release cited them as saying. "It requires sustained efforts to foster respect for diversity, counter incitement to hatred and violence, and create an environment in which all religious or belief communities can live in safety and dignity."
Article Summary: U.N. experts have expressed concerns over reports of human rights violations against members of the Ahmadiyya Muslim community in Pakistan. The experts urged authorities to ensure their protection. They highlighted ongoing attacks on Ahmadi places of worship and desecration of graves.

Article Title: Balochistan’s Zehri under curfew: Civilian killings, detentions and disappearances; what we know
Article Text:
Pakistan's enforced disappearance crisis deepens as four reported missing in Balochistan. Photo credit: ANI

Earlier allegations and UN concerns

A prolonged curfew and reported military operation in Zehri tehsil of Pakistan’s Balochistan province have triggered fresh allegations of detentions, enforced disappearances and civilian casualties.According to a report by The Balochistan Post, Pakistani security forces detained around 25 residents from the Sunni area during the operation and allegedly subjected them to enforced disappearance. Quoting sources,news agency ANI reported that a woman was also killed in a quadcopter attack while she was collecting water, while another woman and a man were wounded.Mobile phone services have reportedly been suspended across Zehri, while residents face restrictions on movement. The Balochistan Post said the area has remained under curfew for months, with residents allowed to leave only during designated hours to purchase essential goods. Travel outside the area reportedly requires authorisation from security forces.The Post also reported that Pakistani forces had allegedly killed more than 20 civilians during an operation in the Sohanda area while the curfew was in force.The latest allegations follow a series of reported enforced disappearances elsewhere in Balochistan.On September 2, the local media reported that four people had allegedly gone missing after being detained in Quetta and Dera Bugti, while four previously reported missing persons were recovered from Karachi, Quetta and Hyderabad.The issue has also drawn concern from UN human rights experts. On Saturday, the Office of the UN high commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) raised concerns over the alleged enforced disappearance, torture and extrajudicial killing of Imran Ali.The UN experts said Ali was abducted from his apartment on August 27, 2025, by around 20 personnel from Pakistan’s Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD). They said people previously detained with him later confirmed that he had been held and allegedly tortured.A police officer reportedly told Pakistan’s Commission of Inquiry on Enforced Disappearances in August 2026 that Ali had been killed during an alleged encounter in May. The UN experts called for an independent investigation, forensic examination and identification of six other bodies reportedly brought to a hospital alongside his remains.Meanwhile, Pakistan’s military said on Friday that its forces had killed 48 militants in raids across Mastung, Sibi, Quetta and Kalat over 72 hours, describing those killed as “Khawarij” and “terrorists” without providing evidence, AP reported.
Article Summary: A prolonged curfew and reported military operation in Zehri tehsil of Pakistan’s Balochistan province have triggered fresh allegations of detentions, enforced disappearances and civilian casualties. Pakistani security forces detained around 25 residents from the Sunni area during the operation and allegedly subjected them to enforced disappearance. A woman was also killed in a quadcopter attack while she was collecting water.

Article Title: ‘Growing differences between military, Asif Zardari’: Self-exiled Pakistani politician Altaf Hussain makes big claim
Article Text:
Self-exiled British-Pakistani politician Altaf Hussain (File photo)

Self-exiled British-Pakistani politician Altaf Hussain has alleged a "silent struggle" is underway between Pakistan's powerful military establishment and President Asif Ali Zardari , warning that a debate over creating new provinces could push the country into a major political and security crisis.The founder of the Muttahida Qaumi Movement (MQM) claimed that discussions were underway on a possible 28th Constitutional Amendment, which could include provisions for the creation of new provinces.“Discussions on the creation of new provinces have been raised by interior minister Mohsin Naqvi and DG-ISPR. The proposed constitutional changes reflect growing differences between President Asif Ali Zardari and the military leadership. A political deadlock could lead to serious constitutional consequences, including the imposition of martial law or the formation of an interim government,” Hussain said in a TikTok message on September 2.Referring to the earlier 26th and 27th Amendments, he alleged that political parties had previously reached agreements to facilitate their passage.Hussain also questioned the prolonged foreign stay of Zardari, the husband of slain former Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto and father of ex-foreign minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari."The President had travelled to Austria in connection for his son Bilawal Zardari’s wedding and is currently in London. There was also an hour-long meeting between Zardari and Naqvi in London, claiming that an important message was conveyed to the President," he added.Hussain further cautioned that tensions between the Pakistan military and Sindhi nationalist groups could escalate into widespread unrest. Referring to the situation in Balochistan, Hussain said violence between security forces and Baloch fighters was continuing and called for greater political consideration for the Baloch people.He warned that if Pakistan descended into a broader civil conflict, foreign powers, including the US and UK, would not come to its rescue, and urged Pakistanis to heed his warnings.
Article Summary: Self-exiled British-Pakistani politician Altaf Hussain has alleged a "silent struggle" is underway between Pakistan's powerful military establishment and President Asif Ali Zardari. The founder of the Muttahida Qaumi Movement (MQM) claimed that discussions were underway on a possible 28th Constitutional Amendment.

Article Title: 25 Pakistani military personnel killed in Balochistan attacks, BLA claims
Article Text:
Balochistan: BLA claims 25 Pakistani military personnel killed in two attacks (Picture from X)

The Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) on Thursday claimed responsibility for two attacks in Pakistan’s Balochistan province, saying 25 Pakistani military personnel were killed and three military vehicles destroyed.According to The Balochistan Post, the BLA spokesperson said fighters targeted a military convoy at Ziarat Cross, attacking vehicles and destroying two of them, including a military truck.The militant group initially claimed that 18 personnel were killed in the attack, with the death toll later rising to 25.The BLA also released a one-minute-and-11-second video trailer through Hakkal, its official media channel, which it said showed footage from the Ziarat Cross attack.The footage purportedly shows armed fighters near burning Pakistani military vehicles, with bodies visible at the site and weapons being seized. The BLA said it would release the complete video later.In a separate operation in the Hajika area of Surab, the group’s Special Tactical Operations Squad (STOS) remotely detonated an explosives-laden vehicle, destroying a military vehicle and killing seven personnel, according to the BLA statement.
Article Summary: Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) claims responsibility for two attacks in Pakistan's Balochistan province. BLA says 25 Pakistani military personnel were killed and three military vehicles destroyed. The militant group also released a one-minute-and-11-second video trailer through Hakkal.

Article Title: ‘6ft by 8ft cell, brown drinking water’: What Imran Khan’s jail cell is like
Article Text:
The report said visitors have been barred and Khan has been confined to his cell for as much as 23 hours a day.

Former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan is being held in what has been described as harsh conditions at Rawalpindi’s Adiala Jail, with reports alleging prolonged isolation, limited access to reading material and restrictions on contact with his family.According to a report by The Times UK, Khan is being kept in a 6ft by 8ft cell typically used for prisoners on death row. The report said the 73-year-old has no reading material apart from the Quran and is being provided “soiled brown water” to drink.His sons, Sulaiman and Kasim Khan, have reportedly been unable to meet their father in person since 2022 and have at times been prevented from speaking to him by telephone for months. They have described his living conditions as inhumane “torture tactics”.The report said visitors have been barred and Khan has been confined to his cell for as much as 23 hours a day.The reported restrictions have also become the subject of repeated legal challenges by Khan’s family.His sister Uzma Khan filed a fresh contempt petition in the Supreme Court on Wednesday, alleging that authorities have failed to comply with an August 18 order concerning Khan’s access to his family.According to The Express Tribune, the petition names Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Adiala Jail Superintendent Sajid Baig, Punjab Inspector General of Prisons Mian Salik Jalal and other senior officials as respondents.The August 18 order had directed authorities to facilitate virtual communication between Khan and his sons and allow his sisters to meet him weekly. However, Uzma said she was denied a scheduled visit on Tuesday, while telephone communication between Khan and his sons has remained restricted since March.The petition also alleges that authorities failed to establish the infrastructure required for bi-weekly telephone calls with Sulaiman and Kasim.The latest dispute follows an earlier contempt petition over the alleged non-compliance with the Supreme Court’s direction to transfer Khan to Shifa International Hospital for medical evaluation. He was instead taken to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) on August 21 before being returned to Adiala Jail after doctors declared him “medically fit”. Authorities have cited security concerns for the decision.
Article Summary: Imran Khan is being held in what has been described as harsh conditions at Rawalpindi’s Adiala Jail. Reports allege prolonged isolation, limited access to reading material and restrictions on contact with his family. His sons, Sulaiman and Kasim Khan, have reportedly been unable to meet their father in person since 2022.

Article Title: Pakistan: Imran Khan's sister files fresh contempt plea over denied jail visits
Article Text: Former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan's sister Uzma Khan on Wednesday filed a fresh contempt of court petition in the Supreme Court, alleging non-enforcement of previous judicial directives issued by the country's apex court.In her petition, Uzma named several high-ranking officials, including Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif and Adiala (Rawalpindi Central Jail) Superintendent Sajid Baig, as respondents.According to the Express Tribune, the petition was filed after the Supreme Court's August 18 instructions, which mandated virtual communication between Imran Khan and his sons, alongside weekly access for his sisters, failed to materialise.The plea said that Uzma Khan was denied a scheduled visit on Tuesday and noted that audio communication with his sons has remained restricted since March.The petition alleged that authorities neglected to establish the necessary infrastructure enabling bi-weekly telephone calls with his sons, Kasim Khan and Sulaiman Khan, as previously ordered by the bench.Earlier, Uzma had filed another contempt application addressing government non-compliance regarding a separate instruction within the August 18 order, which directed that Imran Khan be moved to Shifa International Hospital for medical care.Under the original August 18 decision, the Supreme Court instructed that the former premier be transferred to Shifa International Hospital for clinical evaluation by a multidisciplinary medical panel while simultaneously granting visitation rights.Following the orders, authorities transferred Imran Khan to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) on August 21. He was, however, sent back to Adiala Jail shortly after medical personnel declared him to be "medically fit".Reacting to the developments, the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) lambasted prison administrators for barring relatives from seeing the party founder, characterising the restrictions as a flagrant breach of mandates issued by both the Supreme Court and the Islamabad High Court, as reported by another Pakistan-based daily, Dawn.
Article Summary: Imran Khan's sister Uzma Khan has filed a contempt of court petition in the Supreme Court. She alleges non-enforcement of previous judicial directives issued by the country's apex court. Uzma named several high-ranking officials, including Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif and Adiala (Rawalpindi Central Jail) Superintendent Sajid Baig as respondents.

Article Title: Pak pleads for dialogue after India stands firm on suspending Indus Water Treaty
Article Text:
Indus Waters treaty representational image

India rejects tribunal ruling

Water, terrorism and the SCO

NEW DELHI: Just days after India rejected an international tribunal's ruling on the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) and dismissed its jurisdiction, Pakistan on Wednesday urged New Delhi to engage "constructively" within the framework of the 1960 water-sharing agreement.According to news agency PTI, Pakistan foreign office spokesperson Tahir Andrabi said the Permanent Court of Arbitration had reaffirmed that the treaty remained fully enforced and binding. Pakistan, he said, would take “all possible measures” to ensure the decision was implemented.Andrabi said Pakistan remained committed to implementing the treaty in letter and spirit in accordance with its language and provisions.Pakistan will continue to urge India to reciprocate with the same approach whereby the treaty is upheld in letter and spirit and in its full legal documented provisions, he said, according to PTI.Pakistan had approached the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague in March 2026, seeking a determination on the status of the treaty after India placed it in abeyance.India, however, has consistently rejected the jurisdiction of the arbitration process.On Monday, the ministry of external affairs (MEA) said, “India categorically rejects its so-called award, just as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements by this illegally constituted body.”“India's decision to hold the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance remains in force,” the ministry said.MEA said the Court of Arbitration had issued what it termed an award on May 15, 2026, concerning maximum pondage supplemental to an earlier award on issues of general interpretation of the IWT."This so-called Court was constituted by the World Bank in patent breach of the terms of the Treaty and India categorically rejects its so-called award, just as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements by this illegally constituted body", the ministry stated.India has maintained that the establishment of the arbitral body itself violates the IWT and that it has no jurisdiction over India’s sovereign decision to place the treaty in abeyance.The dispute also featured indirectly at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit, in Bishkek, where Prime Minister Narendra Modi called for action against countries that use terrorism as an instrument of state policy.“We cannot remain confined to an action-reaction approach,” Modi said, calling for the dismantling of terrorist ecosystems, including funding networks, recruitment pipelines and territorial sanctuaries.Pakistan prime minister Shehbaz Sharif, speaking at the summit, described water as the region’s “lifeblood” and said it “must never be weaponised”.“The treaties governing our shared waters are solemn, binding international commitments. They are not matters of political convenience to be cast aside at your will. They must be honoured unconditionally, in both letter and spirit,” Sharif said, according to Dawn.India placed the IWT in abeyance following the April 22, 2025 Pahalgam terror attack, in which 26 people were killed. The Cabinet Committee on Security took the decision on April 23, 2025, with New Delhi saying the conditions underlying the treaty had fundamentally changed.India has said the treaty will remain in abeyance until Pakistan “credibly and irrevocably abjures its support for cross-border terrorism”.
Article Summary: Pakistan urges New Delhi to engage "constructively" within the framework of the 1960 water-sharing agreement. Pakistan had approached the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague in March 2026, seeking a determination on the status of the treaty. India, however, has consistently rejected the jurisdiction of the arbitration process.

Article Title: Leadership gaps cloud Pakistan's human rights oversight system
Article Text:
Pakistan human rights faces pending vacancy

NCHR’s legal status under question

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is most important for an effective human rights body? Strong leadership Independence Transparency Accountability 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan’s human rights oversight framework is facing growing uncertainty as key commissions continue to function without permanent leadership or full membership, raising concerns over their independence and effectiveness.The previous National Commission for Human Rights (NCHR) completed its four-year term in November 2025, but a new commission has yet to be fully constituted, news agency ANI cited in its report. The National Commission on the Status of Women (NCSW) is also functioning under an acting chairperson.Former NCHR chairperson Khawar Mumtaz criticised and warned that prolonged reliance on temporary arrangements could weaken the autonomy and performance of independent rights bodies.Human rights activist Peter Jacob said Parliament passed legislation establishing the National Commission for Minorities Rights in December 2025, but appointments to the body remain incomplete.The National Commission on the Rights of the Child has also faced vacancies. The Ministry of Human Rights invited applications in July 2026 for members representing Punjab, Islamabad and Balochistan, The Express Tribune reported.An amendment to the National Commission for Human Rights Act in 2026 introduced Section 4A, allowing a chairperson to continue for up to 120 days after the expiry of their term or until a successor is appointed.NCHR Chairperson Rabiya Javeri Agha maintained that the commission remains operationally effective, pointing to additional staff recruited two years ago. She said the extension of the chairperson’s tenure was made under the law and reflected practices followed by human rights institutions internationally. Questions regarding the constitution of a new commission, she said, should be directed to the government, according to The Express Tribune.
Article Summary: Pakistan’s human rights oversight framework is facing growing uncertainty. Key commissions continue to function without permanent leadership or full membership. The previous National Commission for Human Rights (NCHR) completed its four-year term in November 2025. A new commission has yet to be fully constituted, news agency ANI cited in its report.

Article Title: Imran Khan, wife Bushra Bibi get slight relief as Pak HC bars solitary confinement
Article Text:
Pak HC intervenes over Imran Khan, wife Bushra Bibi's detention, bars solitary confinement

A Pakistan high court on Tuesday directed authorities at Rawalpindi Jail to ensure that former prime minister Imran Khan and his wife Bushra Bibi are not held in solitary confinement. The ruling also set out provisions for Khan's family meetings, phone calls, reading material and medical care.The Islamabad High Court (IHC), while hearing petitions challenging the couple's alleged solitary confinement, directed the jail authorities to allow Khan's family members to meet him in line with prison rules and arrange telephone conversations with his sons.Justice Khadim Hussain Soomro also ordered the jail to provide Khan with newspapers and books every day and ensure access to medical facilities as prescribed under jail rules. Rawalpindi's Aiala jail superintendent has been asked to implement the directions and submit a compliance report within 15 days, according to the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).The court had earlier reserved its verdict on August 6 on separate petitions filed by Khan's sister Aleema Khanum and Bushra Bibi's daughter Mubashra Khawar Maneka. The IHC also held the petitions challenging the alleged solitary confinement to be maintainable.The 73-year-old cricketer-turned-politician and his wife have been in custody since August 2023 and is serving prison terms in corruption and related cases. Khan's Tehreek-e-Insaf party and supporters have maintained that the cases are politically motivated, while the government has rejected allegations of mistreatment.Bushra Bibi was first jailed in January 2024 after being convicted in a corruption-related case. She was released on bail in October that year after nearly nine months in custody but was arrested again in January 2025 following another corruption conviction. She remains at Adiala Jail.The IHC order comes as Khan's detention and medical treatment remain the subject of separate proceedings before the Supreme Court.On Monday, the Supreme Court declined an application by Khan's sister Uzma Khan seeking an early hearing of her contempt petition against government officials over the alleged failure to comply with an earlier order concerning his transfer to a private hospital, Dawn reported.Pakistan's Supreme Court had on August 18 ordered that Khan be shifted to the privately run Shifa International Hospital after concerns were raised by his family and supporters over his health, including an eye condition diagnosed earlier this year.Instead, Khan was taken to the state-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) on the night of August 20-21 for a medical procedure and diagnostic examinations and was later returned to Adiala Jail.Uzma Khan's petition contends that this breached the Supreme Court's direction that Khan remain admitted at the Islamabad hospital until the next hearing on September 16. The government has defended the decision, citing security concerns.Two specialists from Shifa International Hospital also participated in Khan's eye examination at PIMS, according to the hospital administration, as reported by Dawn.Uzma Khan had sought an earlier hearing, arguing that further delay could affect the enforcement of the Supreme Court's order. The Supreme Court, however, rejected the request under its case-fixation policy, noting that 94 other criminal original petitions in the same category were pending, Dawn reported.The contempt petition is listed for September 16 before a three-member bench comprising Justices Shahid Waheed, Naeem Akhtar Afghan and Ishtiaq Ibrahim. The bench is also scheduled to hear other matters concerning Khan's health and family meetings.
Article Summary: Imran Khan and his wife Bushra Bibi have been in custody since August 2023. The couple is serving prison terms in corruption and related cases. The Islamabad High Court ordered the jail authorities to allow Khan's family members to meet him in line with prison rules.

Article Title: Pakistan power crisis deepens as Karachi reels from 24-hour blackouts
Article Text:
​Karachi reels under deepening power crisis as blackouts last up to 24 hours

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you agree that electricity should be treated as an essential service? Yes No Unsure 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Karachi's electricity crisis has intensified, with residents in several parts of the city reporting outages lasting up to 24 hours. Rights activists in Pakistan have warned that prolonged loadshedding is placing a growing burden on low-income families.According to Dawn, the issue was raised at a press conference at the Karachi Press Club organised by the Civil Society Collective for Clean Energy for Karachi. Speakers said extended power cuts were disrupting basic household activities, education and work, while also worsening access to water and affecting hygiene.Residents of North Karachi, Nazimabad and parts of Gulistan-i-Jauhar reported between 16 and 24 hours of loadshedding, ANI said. Protests and traffic disruptions were also reported in Lyari and other parts of the old city during the week beginning August 24.The speakers cited K-Electric's published outage schedule, saying more than 615 feeders were listed for power cuts of up to 12 hours a day. They claimed this could affect nearly a third of the city's feeders.Qazi Khizer of the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan said the prolonged outages were having a particularly severe impact on working-class communities.He said electricity shortages were also contributing to rising mental stress and argued that reliable electricity "should be treated as an essential service rather than a privilege".Karachi Union of Journalists president Tahir Hassan Khan questioned whether K-Electric's privatisation had delivered the improvements promised to consumers.He said claims of technological and operational progress had not translated into "dependable electricity supplies".
Article Summary: Residents of North Karachi, Nazimabad and parts of Gulistan-i-Jauhar reported between 16 and 24 hours of loadshedding. Protests and traffic disruptions were also reported in Lyari and other parts of the old city during the week beginning August 24.

Article Title: Pakistan court allows Hindu woman to return home after alleged forced conversion, marriage
Article Text:
Woman returns from Pakistan

'Want to return home'

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe that the court made the right decision in allowing Reeta to return to her parents? Yes, it was the right decision. No, she should have been placed in shelter. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A court in Pakistan on Tuesday allowed a 21-year-old Hindu woman to return to her parents after she told the magistrate that she wished to go home of her own free will, days after her family alleged that she had been abducted and pressured to convert to Islam and marry a Muslim man, news agency PTI reported.Shirimati Reeta, a resident of Rana Rajput Colony in Khipro tehsil of Sindh’s Sanghar district, went missing from her hometown last week, according to a complaint filed by her brother Ravi Shankar. He alleged that CCTV footage showed unidentified people taking Reeta from the family home along with valuables and mobile phones on August 24.According to the complaint, Reeta was taken to Gujranwala in Punjab, some 80 kms from Lahore, where she was allegedly pressured to convert to Islam and marry Nazeer Hussain, who was already married.Punjab Police later recovered Reeta and produced her before a judicial magistrate on Monday. The investigating officer sought to place her in Darul Aman, a state-run shelter, claiming that she was unwilling to return to her parents.Her lawyers, Asad Jamal and Kheta Ram, opposed the request and told the court that Reeta wanted to return home with her brother, who was present in court, a court official said.The magistrate then asked Reeta to record her statement under oath. “In her statement, Reeta said that she wanted to return to her parents’ home of her own free will,” the official said.The court subsequently allowed Reeta to leave with her brother and made him responsible for her safe custody and transportation back to the family home in Sanghar.
Article Summary: Shirimati Reeta, a 21-year-old Hindu woman, went missing from her hometown last week. Her family alleged that she had been abducted and pressured to convert to Islam and marry a Muslim man. Police later recovered Reeta and produced her before a judicial magistrate on Monday. The investigating officer sought to place her in Darul Aman, a state-run shelter.

Article Title: Watch: 'Driverless' car crashes into police van after internet outage in Islamabad
Article Text:
In a social media post on Monday, Aalijah sought to clarify that his video was not intended to ridicule Zafar or undermine his work and warned that the technology was not yet ready to be considered completely reliable.

A remotely operated driverless car crashed into a police van in Islamabad after losing its internet connection during a demonstration, with footage of the incident going viral and sparking a wave of memes online.According to local media, the incident took place at D-Chowk, a high-security area in the Pakistani capital, where journalist Muhammad Aalijah was recording a video of a technology-based automated-driving system developed by Abbottabad-based technology enthusiast Ehsan Zafar. The car was being controlled remotely over the internet when a sudden connectivity failure caused its steering to malfunction.Footage shared by Aalijah shows him sitting in the front passenger seat as he explains the vehicle's features while it moves along the road. The remotely controlled steering wheel then appears to lose control, sending the car towards a police van parked nearby.Aalijah can be seen attempting to stop the vehicle by pulling the handbrake, but the car continues moving and bumps into the police vehicle.Aalijah later told Dawn that he had been asked by Zafar to report on his technology-based automated-driving innovation. He attributed the crash to a "technical fault" triggered by an internet disruption.“Everything was fine until a technical fault occurred due to an internet disruption, causing the car to go out of control and crash into a police vehicle,” he said.According to Aalijah, the vehicle was operated remotely through internet and satellite connections. The loss of the internet connection during the demonstration caused the car to become uncontrollable.In a social media post on Monday, Aalijah sought to clarify that his video was not intended to ridicule Zafar or undermine his work.“The sole purpose was to raise awareness and urge people to remain cautious until any new experiment or technology has been thoroughly tested, proven safe and established as a complete success,” he said.“This was a message of caution, not an attempt to discredit anyone.”Aalijah also warned that the technology was not yet ready to be considered completely reliable.“The vehicle was being operated through satellite and internet connections, but during external control, it went out of control as soon as the internet connection was disconnected and collided with a police vehicle,” he wrote.He said the relatively low traffic at D-Chowk limited the potential consequences of the malfunction, but warned that a similar failure on a busy road could have been far more serious.“If the same situation had occurred on a busy road, the consequences could have been extremely dangerous, even fatal,” he said.“This video is not criticism; it is a responsible effort to raise awareness and issue a warning by all means, experiment, but ensure safety first,” he added.
Article Summary: A remotely operated driverless car crashed into a police van in Islamabad after losing its internet connection during a demonstration. The incident took place at D-Chowk, a high-security area in the Pakistani capital. The car was being controlled remotely over the internet when a sudden connectivity failure caused its steering to malfunction. Footage of the incident went viral and sparked a wave of memes online.

Article Title: Pak PM scrambles for damage control after his office edits leaders out of SCO summit photo
Article Text:
The edited framing keeps Sharif at the centre alongside several prominent leaders

What’s was on the agenda

What

PM Modi

told SCO summit

Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif appeared to go into damage-control mode on Tuesday after his office shared an edited version of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit’s family photograph, cropping out several world leaders while keeping Sharif prominently at the centre of the frame.The Pakistan Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) first shared the edited summit photograph at 11:42am IST.The full image showed the heads of SCO member states and senior officials standing together ahead of a session of the 26th SCO Summit in Bishkek.From left, the photograph featured SCO Secretary-General Nurlan Yermekbayev, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Tajik President Emomali Rahmon, Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and SCO Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure chief Ularbek Sharsheev.The selective framing put Sharif at the centre of the image alongside several prominent leaders.At 3.32pm IST, the Pakistani Prime Minister shared the full family photograph featuring all the world leaders.The 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Leadership Summit focused on strengthening regional cooperation and addressing shared security, economic and geopolitical challenges.The summit, marking the SCO’s 25th anniversary was held in the expanded “SCO Plus” format, bringing together leaders from member, partner and observer countries to discuss wider regional and global issuesDuring the summit, PM Modi addressed the SCO summit and called for a united fight against terrorism, saying there could be no “double standards” on the issue.“We must dismantle the entire ecosystem of terrorism--its financing, recruitment, radicalisation, and safe havens,” Modi said, adding that countries which use terrorism as an instrument of policy and provide shelter or support to terrorists must be sent a strong message.PM Modi also called for greater regional cooperation on security, connectivity and economic opportunities, while stressing dialogue and diplomacy as the way forward in addressing conflicts.
Article Summary: Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif appeared to go into damage-control mode on Tuesday. His office shared an edited version of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit’s family photograph, cropping out several world leaders. The selective framing put Sharif at the centre of the image alongside several prominent leaders.

Article Title: 100-year-old Hindu temple demolished in Pakistan’s Punjab
Article Text:
PMMP chairman Aslam Parvez Sahotra said he met Punjab Additional Home Secretary on August 28 and submitted a written application seeking action against those allegedly responsible for the demolition, as well as officials accused of failing to protect the property.

Poll Vote & Share your view What steps should be prioritized to protect religious heritage sites? Stronger security and monitoring Government protection and restoration Community engagement and awareness programs 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A more than 100-year-old Hindu temple in Pakistan ’s Punjab province was demolished on August 21 in Siraj village of Narowal, around 130 km from Lahore, with minority groups alleging that religious zealots targeted the site to absorb its land into an adjacent madrassa. The government, however, has maintained that the temple collapsed because of torrential rains.The demolition has triggered demands for an investigation and restoration of the temple, with the Pakistan Masiha Millat Party (PMMP) accusing local authorities and the Evacuee Trust Property Board (ETPB) of failing to protect the centuries-old Hindu place of worship.PMMP chairman Aslam Parvez Sahotra said he met Punjab Additional Home Secretary on August 28 and submitted a written application seeking action against those allegedly responsible for the demolition, as well as officials accused of failing to protect the property.Sahotra alleged that the people involved in the demolition were associated with the Tehreek-i-Labbaik Pakistan (TLP), a banned far-right Islamic party. He further claimed that after the temple was brought down, metal fittings from its shikhar, bricks and other material were removed from the site.The temple, estimated to be between 100 and 125 years old, stood on approximately 1,000 square metres of land in Siraj village.The dispute over the site predates its demolition. According to Sahotra, land adjoining the temple had earlier been leased by the ETPB for a madrassa. The lease was subsequently cancelled after rent allegedly went unpaid for several years and the premises were not used for the stated purpose.He said several people later occupied portions of the property illegally.Sahotra referred to a revenue department report which identified individuals as illegal occupants of the temple’s quarters and other parts of the property. He said the ETPB deputy administrator in Sialkot cancelled the seminary’s lease rights on January 29, 2026, and ordered the eviction of illegal occupants and sealing of the property.“This order was not implemented,” Sahotra alleged.A report attributed to the DSP Narowal, dated April 11, also indicated that local police were aware of security concerns surrounding the temple and the possibility that it could be damaged, according to Sahotra.The ETPB, however, has rejected the allegation that the temple was deliberately demolished.ETPB senior official Rana Iftikhar told PTI that the temple had collapsed following torrential rains. He acknowledged its historical significance, saying, “The temple carries no name in our record books. However, it is a very old one... more than 100 to 125 years old,” he said.Iftikhar also confirmed that the land adjoining the temple had been leased for a seminary, but maintained that the temple's own land had not been leased.“However, the temple's land is not given to anyone for lease,” he said and added the ETPB highups will decide about restoration of the temple.The conflicting accounts have heightened concerns among members of the local Hindu community.Hindu community leader Rattan Lal condemned the demolition and called for the government to order the temple's restoration. He said the district administration and ETPB had failed to take adequate steps to secure the site or remove alleged illegal occupants.“The district administration and the ETPB failed to take adequate measures to protect the site or remove the alleged occupants, ultimately allowing the temple to be demolished,” Lal said and asked the government to take action against those found involved in the demolition of the temple.Lal, who is also a Hindu member of the Narowal District Peace Committee and the Pak Dharam Astan Hindu Committee, said members of the community were now reluctant to approach the site.“We are even afraid to visit the site because of the madrassa that continues to operate on its premises.”Sahotra has called for the temple to be rebuilt in its original form and urged the Punjab government to strengthen protection for Hindu temples, Sikh gurdwaras and Christian churches, along with their adjoining properties.Arya, meanwhile, said decades of conflict between Pakistan and India, the Islamisation policies of the 1980s and the 1992 demolition of the Babri Masjid in India had contributed to a sense of insecurity among local Hindus.“Preserving Hindu heritage can improve the image of Pakistan and attract tourism.”
Article Summary: More than 100-year-old Hindu temple in Pakistan's Punjab province was demolished on August 21. Minority groups claim the temple was demolished to make way for an Islamic madrassa. The Pakistan Masiha Millat Party (PMMP) has submitted a written application seeking action against those allegedly responsible.

Article Title: Lahore inflation squeezes household budgets as food, rent and utility costs rise
Article Text:
People walk through a market to shop for grocery and other items

Vegetable, LPG prices add to public anger

Rising inflation in Pakistan's Lahore has intensified financial pressures on ordinary citizens, with soaring prices of food, rent, utilities and other essentials making it increasingly difficult for low-income families to make ends meet, new agency ANI reported.Residents said the rising cost of basic commodities has made it difficult for some households to afford even two meals a day. Prices of flour, cooking oil, pulses, vegetables and other necessities have continued to rise, while daily-wage workers and low-income earners said their incomes have failed to keep pace with inflation.Citizens also raised concerns over sharply higher vegetable prices, saying commonly consumed items such as potatoes and tomatoes have become increasingly unaffordable. Residents said vegetables were being sold for around Rs 150 to Rs 300 per kilogram, depending on the item and market.One resident appealed to the government to address the difficulties faced by poor families, saying rising food prices, rent and utility bills had made household management extremely challenging. Families on limited incomes, he said, were increasingly being forced to choose between food, rent, medicines and other essential expenses.ANI reports that people living on modest pensions were struggling to manage household expenses, particularly when they also had children, medical costs and other financial responsibilities.Residents also criticised the government over LPG prices, alleging that the fuel was being sold above official rates in some markets. They questioned who would regulate traders and ensure enforcement of government price controls.Rickshaw driver Usman Ali said rising fuel and essential commodity prices had severely affected his livelihood, leaving little or nothing to save after meeting basic household expenses.Citizens further questioned why lower petrol prices had not resulted in cheaper food and other essential commodities, asking why reductions in fuel costs were not being reflected in market prices.
Article Summary: Rising prices of food, rent, utilities and other essentials making it increasingly difficult for low-income families to make ends meet. Prices of flour, cooking oil, pulses, vegetables and other necessities have continued to rise. Citizens also raised concerns over sharply higher vegetable prices. Residents also criticised the government over LPG prices.

Article Title: Bangladesh and India plan to resume train ops by October
Article Text:
Bangladesh and India plan to resume train ops by October

Poll Vote & Share your view Which train service are you most looking forward to resuming? Maitree Express Mitali Express Bandhan Express 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

DHAKA: Bangladesh and India plan to resume cross-border train operations through the Maitree, Mitali and Bandhan Express trains by Oct and the annual meeting of railway authorities of the two countries beginning Tuesday will work in that direction, officials have said.Since the fall of Sheikh Hasina's govt on Aug 5, 2024, and the resulting political change, normalcy has gradually returned to Bangladesh. However, passenger train services between Bangladesh and India have not resumed - the suspension of the Maitree, Bandhan and Mitali Express services was officially announced on July 19, 2024.The two-day meeting between the railway authorities of the two neighbours will begin in Dhaka on Tuesday, Bangladesh railway sources said. "We don't only share borders, we share dreams. I am repeating the same thing - people-to-people relationships are important, and we are absolutely confident that at the right time (the PM's visit will take place). The Prime Minister of Bangladesh has a standing invitation, and he knows it," Indian high commissioner to Bangladesh Dinesh Trivedi said on Monday.In addition to restarting the three trains, Bangladesh will propose launching a new train service from Rajshahi to Kolkata. Bangladesh is interested in operating Maitree Express between Dhaka and Kolkata via the Padma Bridge, which was opened during the Sheikh Hasina era. Until now, the train has operated via the Jamuna Bridge.
Article Summary: Bangladesh and India plan to resume cross-border train operations by October 2024. Annual meeting of railway authorities of the two countries beginning Tuesday will work in that direction. Maitree, Mitali and Bandhan Express trains were suspended on July 19, 2024.

Article Title: People stealing valuables from dead bodies in Nepal floods; police issue warning
Article Text: Nepal Police have warned people against keeping, selling or distributing valuables recovered from flood-hit areas, urging them to hand over such items to the authorities.In a statement issued on Sunday, police said using, concealing, buying or selling valuables found during the floods could constitute an offence and invite legal action.The police also cautioned that disasters can create conditions for increased theft, looting and fraud as security personnel remain engaged in search-and-rescue operations.The warning came days after 29 people were arrested in Dhading for allegedly breaking open a vault that had been swept downstream from Rasuwa and the upper catchment areas and taking cash from it.A joint patrol team of the Armed Police Force and Nepal Police reportedly caught the suspects at the site while they were allegedly extracting money from the damaged safe.In another case, Nepal Police arrested two men for allegedly stealing gold earrings from the body of a woman who was swept downstream by floods in the Narayani River. The incident came to light after a video of it went viral on social media.The police warning was not linked to any specific incident but came amid a series of reports of valuables being recovered from areas devastated by the floods.Flash floods triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26 devastated towns and villages across northern and central Nepal.The Bhotekoshi River, flowing south from the Himalayan border region, carried the floodwaters downstream, sweeping away homes, vehicles, roads and bridges and damaging hydropower projects.The disaster has killed more than 1,300 people, while around 5,000 remain missing.
Article Summary: Nepal Police have warned people against keeping, selling or distributing valuables recovered from flood-hit areas. The warning came days after 29 people were arrested for allegedly breaking open a vault that had been swept downstream from Rasuwa and the upper catchment areas.

Article Title: Nepal marks the 13th day of mourning after deadly flash floods
Article Text:
Nepal observed a national day of mourning on Monday, 13 days after the devastating Rasuwa flash floods.

Nepal observed a national day of mourning on Monday, 13 days after the devastating Rasuwa flash floods, as the country paid tribute to more than 1,355 people killed in one of its deadliest natural disasters in recent history.Nearly 5,000 people remain missing, including 589 foreign nationals, following the flash floods that struck Rasuwa, a district bordering China, and neighbouring areas on August 26.The disaster was triggered by an ice-rock avalanche in the high Himalayas, unleashing powerful floodwaters that caused widespread loss of life and extensive damage to infrastructure across northern and central Nepal.According to the PTI report, Nepal has declared September 7 a national day of mourning to honour victims of the devastating floods that swept through Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and other areas along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli river systems.The observance falls on the 13th day after the disaster, reflecting the traditional Hindu practice of marking the thirteenth day following a death. In many Hindu communities, the day is considered highly significant to honor the deceased members and the also mark the conclusion of the formal mourning period.The Ministry of Home Affairs said the national flag would be flown at half-mast at government offices across Nepal as well as at Nepali diplomatic missions abroad.The floods caused widespread loss of life and severe damage to homes and vital infrastructure, including roads, bridges, hydropower projects and government buildings.Search and rescue operations remain underway in the hardest-hit areas, including tunnels at hydropower projects, as security personnel and specialised international rescue teams continue efforts to locate missing people and recover bodies.At least 32,000 families have been displaced, while around 7,500 homes were completely destroyed. The disaster has also disrupted livelihoods and damaged essential infrastructure across central Nepal.The government has deployed the Nepali Army, Nepal Police, Armed Police Force and other agencies to carry out search, rescue, relief and recovery operations.Specialist teams from neighbouring countries, including India, have joined the rescue efforts, particularly operations to save people believed to be trapped inside hydropower tunnels.Meanwhile, the Nepal government has declared Tuesday, September 8, a public holiday to commemorate Gen Z Martyrs’ Day, marking a year since the youth-led protests that reshaped the country’s political landscape.The protests erupted in Kathmandu on the same day last year after the government banned several social media platforms. Demonstrators also took to the streets over alleged corruption and what they described as the lavish lifestyles of the children of powerful politicians and government officials.The protests intensified after security forces opened fire near the Parliament building, killing 72 people, including children. The escalating unrest eventually prompted then-Prime Minister K P Sharma Oli to resign.The political fallout resulted in the dissolution of Parliament and the collapse of the coalition government led by the CPN-UML and Nepali Congress. A caretaker administration was subsequently installed, paving the way for fresh parliamentary elections on March 5 this year.The election brought the Gen Z-backed Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), led by Rabi Lamichhane, to power with an almost two-thirds majority. Former Kathmandu mayor Balendra Shah subsequently became prime minister.
Article Summary: Nearly 5,000 people remain missing, including 589 foreign nationals, following the flash floods that struck Rasuwa, a district bordering China, and neighbouring areas on August 26. The disaster was triggered by an ice-rock avalanche in the high Himalayas, unleashing powerful floodwaters that caused widespread loss of life.

Article Title: Climate justice tops agenda as Nepal PM Balen flies to UN office
Article Text:
Nepal PM Balendra Shah

KATHMANDU: Nepal PM Balendra Shah will make his first foreign trip almost six months after taking office when he travels to New York later this month for the 81st UN General Assembly, where Nepal's Bhote Koshi-Trishuli disaster is expected to anchor his push for climate justice, reconstruction assistance and stronger international protection for the Himalayan region. Shah assumed office on March 27 and has so far travelled neither to India nor China, breaking bilateral traditions.Singha Darbar had initially planned to send foreign minister Shisir Khanal to lead Nepal's delegation, but the scale of the flood prompted calls within the ruling establishment and outside it for Shah himself to take Nepal's case before world leaders. The high-level UN General Debate begins Sept 22.Shah has already framed the disaster in global terms. "Climate change is a global problem," he said while speaking about the flood this week. "Mitigating and managing its impacts is a shared responsibility of the international community." In a separate statement, he said it was time for Nepal to "strongly raise" before the international community the disasters the country was facing because of climate change.Climate experts want him to go further in New York and make a specific case for compensation and climate finance, rather than limit his intervention to appeals for assistance. "Nepal is paying the price for a crisis it didn't create," climate policy expert Aarti Khosla said, saying the disaster showed why climate action had to be placed at the centre of development planning.Former finance minister Barshaman Pun, who submitted a set of recommendations to Shah, has urged him to demand compensation for losses caused by rising global temperatures and carbon emissions.
Article Summary: Nepal PM Balendra Shah will make his first foreign trip almost six months after taking office. Shah assumed office on March 27 and has so far travelled neither to India nor China. The Bhote Koshi-Trishuli disaster is expected to anchor his push for climate justice.

Article Title: Need good working ties with India: Bangladesh
Article Text:
Bangladesh wants engagement and good working relationship with India

DHAKA: Bangladesh wants engagement and good working relationship with India despite existing challenges, state minister for foreign affairs Humayun Kobir said Saturday, seeking continued dialogue with New Delhi.His remarks come amid strained ties between the neighbours over issues such as former PM Sheikh Hasina's extradition and Dhaka growing cooperation with China and Pakistan.Foreign, economic and security cooperation and policies are intertwined and interrelated for most countries around the world, not just for Bangladesh, Kobir said."It cannot be isolated from each other. Particularly, for the foreign policy that we have undertaken, it has to be integrated and it must be complementary to each other. From that point of view, foreign policy is not about only foreign relations. There needs to be a strong area of engagement for economic cooperation," he said.Kobir said the door for dialogue will always remain open. "There might be thousands of problems and challenges with India, but the door of dialogue and discussion will always remain open. And that should be kept," he told reporters in Sylhet.
Article Summary: Bangladesh wants engagement and good working relationship with India. State minister for foreign affairs Humayun Kobir seeking continued dialogue with New Delhi. Remarks come amid strained ties between the neighbours over issues such as former PM Sheikh Hasina's extradition and Dhaka growing cooperation with China and Pakistan.

Article Title: 10 days after Nepal flash floods, woman, Chinese man rescued
Article Text:
Two people were rescued alive from separate flood-hit sites on Saturday
